name: diagnose-dont-shortcut-build-drift
description: "For build/output nondeterminism bugs (design-token pilot and similar), isolate root cause via pinned reproduction rather than reaching for a manual edit or platform-specific exception"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: d5f1a2d2-b57b-4f4d-832a-807fb60b9c83
  modified: 2026-09-13T07:41:05.043Z
---

When a build/pipeline produces an unexpected diff (e.g. the 2026-09-13 Node 20.15→22.4 web key-ordering diff in [[project_anya_design_token_pilot]]), the validated approach is: pin the suspect variable (runtime version, locale/ICU, etc.), reproduce byte-identical output from the unchanged canonical/source input in a scratch dir, confirm the diff is order/formatting-only vs. real content change, then fix the actual root cause (e.g. enforce explicit canonical sort before serialization) — not a manual data edit and not a platform- or version-specific carve-out.

**Why:** User explicitly praised this sequence (pin runtime+locale, byte-identical repro, root-cause fix, no manual edit, no platform-specific exception) and specifically valued that it was carried through end-to-end within the owner's/assistant's own lane rather than deferring back and turning the user into a routine reviewer.
**How to apply:** Applies broadly to build-determinism/drift-check bugs, not just this one pilot: prefer isolate-then-root-cause-fix over quick patches, avoid platform- or version-specific exceptions as fixes, and when work is within scope, drive it to a finished fix rather than punting back for review at each step.

name: feedback-metrics-router-go-conventions
description: "Standing Go code conventions for metrics-router since last year's rewrite: gofmt strict, table-driven tests on routing logic, no log.Fatal in handlers"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 3b1f73fb-de26-4dd4-9f24-cf5dd04ef029
  modified: 2026-09-12T06:34:37.697Z
---

Any code that stays in metrics-router should follow these standing conventions, in place since last year's rewrite:
- gofmt strict (no deviations from gofmt output)
- table-driven tests for routing logic
- no `log.Fatal` in handlers

**Why:** User doesn't want request-handling code able to decide the process dies — that's a process-lifecycle decision, not something a handler should own.

**How to apply:** Apply these conventions when writing or reviewing any metrics-router Go code, not just the current config-loader cleanup ([[project_metrics_router_config_loader_cleanup]]). Flag `log.Fatal` (or equivalent process-killing calls) found in handler code as a convention violation.

  type: feedback
  originSessionId: ab05abb8-e445-4ff4-8af2-a2ad9e5a4d67

Never schedule or suggest production deploys (including staging cutovers) for Friday afternoon. Friday afternoon is reserved for code review and prep; any cutover or deploy should be held until Monday morning.

**Why:** User was burned by an outage from a Friday deploy at their prior job in Q4 2021, and has kept this as a standing personal rule since.

**How to apply:** When planning rollout timing for [[project_metrics_router_migration]] or any other prod change, default to Monday-morning (or otherwise non-Friday-afternoon) windows unless the user explicitly says otherwise.

**Update, 2023-04-28 — now team-wide policy at Sphere:** As one of the mitigations to come out of the INC-2023-04-18-001 postmortem review (see [[project_shard_keeper_label_map_cutover]]), "no Friday-afternoon prod deploys" was formally adopted as a team-wide rule, not just the user's personal practice.

**How to apply:** This is no longer just an individual quirk to accommodate — it's an official team policy, so it applies to any teammate's deploy planning discussed with the user, not only the user's own changes.

name: feedback-protect-quiet-evenings
description: "Don't treat unexpectedly free personal time (evenings, weekend mornings) as bonus work time, especially for Lantern"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 780094f0-f0af-443b-a25c-49bfcb1874b8
  modified: 2026-09-12T09:49:20.874Z
---

When personal time opens up — an evening freed early (e.g. Devika's hospital day ending, 2023-08-09) or a quiet weekend morning (e.g. 2026-08-13 Sunday post-Lantern-week: cortado, crossword, breakfast with Devika) — the user's default instinct is to fill it with extra work, usually [[project_lantern_observability_sketch]] polishing, and he's explicitly chosen not to each time, sometimes naming it upfront ("not opening Lantern dashboards, not using the quiet apartment as a fake work block").

**Why:** He wants downtime to actually stay downtime, not get absorbed into demo/feature polishing just because the space is calm and the work is available. This is about protecting rest broadly, not a one-off evening or a specific task.

**How to apply:** Don't propose or encourage using any freed-up personal time (evenings, weekend mornings, unexpected gaps) for extra Lantern work or similar polishing tasks. If he flags quiet personal time, affirm it and don't pivot to work suggestions — let him lead if he wants to bring work up himself.

**Update (2026-09-12 21:15 ET):** Same evening as the [[project_lantern_observability_sketch]] raw-notes boundary decision, user came home "drained, not angry" — the decision itself landed cleanly, but keeping Product Engineering from feeling shut down cost real social energy. Explicitly decided not to reopen the Lantern thread absent a real page; laptop closed, dinner at home. Reinforces the pattern: even when the day's work outcome was good, he still deliberately declines to convert leftover adrenaline into more work.

**How to apply:** When a workday resolves well but visibly cost social/emotional effort, don't read that as an opening to help him "wrap up loose ends" or process it via more work — the instinct to protect the evening applies to good outcomes too, not just stressful/unresolved ones.

Sphere's 2028 open-enrollment preview was posted 2027-09-10; full comparison details (incl. OOP max and network) published 2027-09-21. Election deadline: **2027-10-22 5:00 PM Eastern**.

Posted 2028 individual plan terms:
- HDHP: $104/biweekly paycheck ($2,704/yr over 26 checks); $2,400 deductible; 10% coinsurance after deductible; **$4,800 out-of-pocket max**; preventive fully covered; HSA-eligible. Employer HSA funding confirmed 2027-09-15: $900/yr via four $225 deposits in January, April, July, and October — same structure as 2027 (see [[project_2027_open_enrollment_decision]]).
- PPO: $171/biweekly paycheck ($4,446/yr); $800 deductible; 20% coinsurance after deductible; **$3,500 out-of-pocket max**; preventive fully covered; not HSA-eligible.
- Network: Alex's current primary-care office and preferred pharmacy are in-network under **both** plans — network is not a differentiator for this decision.

Full-year cost comparison (premium + out-of-pocket), all spend levels resolved now that OOP maxes are known:
- Low/typical spend: HDHP's $1,742/yr premium advantage exceeds the $1,600 deductible gap, and HDHP's lower 10% (vs 20%) coinsurance means PPO never catches up before either plan's deductible+coinsurance phase ends.
- Worst case (hits OOP max): HDHP total = $2,704 premium + $4,800 OOP max = $7,504, minus $900 employer HSA funding = **$6,604 net**. PPO total = $4,446 premium + $3,500 OOP max = **$7,946**, no HSA offset. HDHP is cheaper by $1,342 even in the worst-case catastrophic scenario (still cheaper by $442 comparing gross costs alone, before the HSA credit).
- **Conclusion: HDHP is cheaper than PPO at every spend level, from $0 to worst-case.** The previously open question (whether an unknown OOP max could flip the picture at high spend) is now resolved — it doesn't.

**Why:** Recurring annual decision, same self-service pattern as [[project_2027_open_enrollment_decision]] and [[project_2026_hdhp_enrollment_decision]] — Alex has chosen HDHP+HSA both prior cycles.

**How to apply:** If Alex asks to revisit this, the math now strongly favors HDHP at every spend level with no remaining unknowns on cost or network — no need to re-derive unless plan terms change. Still open: (1) Alex's own per-paycheck HSA contribution amount is a separate, lower-stakes decision that can be adjusted later in the plan year (per 2027 FAQ), (2) election not yet submitted as of 2027-10-10 (Alex has asked to leave it undecided for now). This doesn't affect Alex's current 2027 HDHP election, $90/paycheck contribution, remaining 2027 October employer deposit, or [[project_hsa_investment_liquidity_threshold]] auto-invest setting.

**RESOLVED 2027-10-20:** Alex personally completed and submitted the 2028 election during the reserved block, ahead of the 2027-10-22 5:00 PM ET deadline. Portal shows the election as submitted and final:
- Individual HDHP, 2028-01-01 through 2028-12-31, $104/biweekly paycheck ($2,704/yr over 26 checks); $2,400 deductible; 10% coinsurance after deductible; $4,800 OOP max; preventive fully covered; HSA-eligible.
- Current primary-care office and preferred pharmacy confirmed in-network.
- Employee HSA contribution elected: $90/paycheck × 26 = $2,340/yr.
- Employer HSA funding: four $225 deposits (Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct) = $900/yr.
- Combined planned 2028 HSA funding: $3,240.
- 2027 coverage and payroll settings remain unchanged through 2027-12-31.

name: anya-design-token-pilot
description: "Anya's North Pier design-token pilot — ADOPTED 2026-09-13 as ongoing workflow; she is confirmed owner of the design-system/engineering-handoff lane"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

---

On 2024-04-18, Anya's first-month audit at North Pier found conflicting color/spacing token names between Figma and the manually maintained engineering JSON. North Pier accepted her proposal for a six-week pilot: one versioned machine-readable token package is canonical, downstream representations (engineering JSON, Figma-facing) are generated from it, and an automated CI drift check detects divergence. It is a pilot, not yet North Pier's standard workflow, and Anya owns the proposal and rollout.

User reviewed her failure-behavior draft (pinned canonical version → generate both reps into a temp dir → block publish on generator failure or drift → no branch commits/rewrites → publish only if both generators succeed and drift check is clean). Overall shape judged sound (fail-closed, isolated, no silent rewrites). Flagged for tightening: distinguish "exited 0" from "produced valid non-empty/schema-valid output," make sure timeouts/OOM kills count as failures, make the publish step a hard CI pipeline dependency rather than a convention, and consider stale-pin/concurrent-run ordering at publish time.

On 2024-04-23, Anya ran the pilot's first failure-path exercise: the CSS generator wrote directly into the real output directory before platform-JSON validation failed, so registry publication never ran but the workspace was left with mixed old/new generated files (risk of accidental partial commit). This is a gap between her original spec (generate into temp dir, block publish on failure/drift) and the actual generator's write path. User sanity-checked a fail-closed fix: route all generators (including CSS) through temp/staging only, promote to the real output dir via one atomic move only after all generators + validation succeed, delete staging and leave real output untouched on any failure (including timeout/OOM), and keep staging outside git's reach as defense in depth.

On 2024-04-30, the drift check itself produced a false positive: running the generator twice from the same canonical package gave byte-different Android JSON because one map serializes in traversal order (not sorted). Semantic content was identical; the drift check hashes raw output, so it flagged drift on roughly 1 in 4 runs. Nothing was published, and the fail-closed staging-directory behavior (from the 2024-04-23 fix) held correctly. User's sanity-check: fix both — deterministic key ordering in the generator (hygiene/reproducibility, not sufficient alone) plus replacing the drift check's hash comparison with semantic (parse-then-deep-equal) comparison, since hash comparison is inherently fragile to any future formatting variance. Specified tests: generator determinism regression, drift-check true-negative (reordered/reformatted-but-identical content), true-positive mutations (value change, key add/remove), type-sensitivity (e.g. `"4"` vs `4`), and a fail-closed regression test to ensure the semantic layer doesn't loosen publication safety.

On 2024-05-14, a second North Pier team's first workflow run hit a generator/schema version mismatch: CI resolved generator 0.9.0 (requires schema_version >= 3) against the canonical package's schema_version 2 (matching the consumer's 0.8.4 lockfile pin). The generator correctly refused to run; publication was skipped and staging artifacts were removed. Canonical package untouched, nothing published, prior 0.8.4 outputs still matched the semantic fixture — a pinning/CI-resolution gap (generator pin floated ahead of schema), not a broken generator or drift. User's fix: pin the generator to an exact version (not a range) matching current schema_version, add an explicit pre-flight compatibility check in CI as a named failure distinct from the generator's own runtime error, and treat schema bumps as a two-step coordinated migration (bump canonical schema_version + validate first, only then bump the CI generator pin) rather than letting generator and schema versions move independently. Not called adopted.

On 2024-05-27, the same class of false positive recurred one layer up: packaging the canonical schema-3 output into a distributable ZIP gave different archive hashes on Linux vs macOS (different entry order, different per-entry timestamps), even though extracted file contents and permissions matched exactly. Generator/canonical package both still pinned at 0.9.0; nothing published; fail-closed held (publish blocked on any hash mismatch). Diagnosis: not content drift, but archive-level packaging nondeterminism (OS-dependent directory-traversal order feeding entry order; build-time wall-clock mtime feeding per-entry timestamps) — same shape as the 2024-04-30 map-serialization-order bug, recurring at the packaging step instead of the generator step. User's fix, mirroring 04-30: (a) deterministic packaging — canonical sorted entry order, fixed non-wall-clock timestamps (e.g. constant epoch or version-tied SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH), explicit mode/uid/gid instead of host defaults, fixed compression settings, no host-specific extra fields; (b) don't gate publish on raw archive-hash equality even after (a) — replace with semantic comparison at the archive layer (canonicalized/sorted entry-path-set equality + per-entry deep-equal content comparator + explicit mode check), keeping raw hash only as an optional secondary reproducibility check. Added as a permanent regression case in the drift-check suite. Not yet confirmed adopted.

On 2026-09-13 (earlier in the day), after sorting entries and normalizing timestamps per the 2024-05-27 fix, Linux and macOS archives now match byte-for-byte, but Windows still differs: extracted content and entry order are identical, but the Windows-native zip writer adds a `0x000a` NTFS extra field (36 bytes/entry) that Linux/macOS don't write. Publication still blocked (fail-closed held correctly). User's recommendation: (a) root-cause fix — stop using platform-native zip tooling on the Windows runner (PowerShell `Compress-Archive`/.NET `ZipFile` are the likely source) and instead run the same zip-writing implementation across all three runners, with each entry's extra field explicitly forced empty, achieving true byte-identical archives; (b) regardless of (a), don't gate publish on raw hash — this is the same "raw hash is fragile to incidental tool/metadata variance" pattern from 2024-04-30 and 2024-05-27, now a third recurrence, and reinforces adopting the semantic archive-layer gate (entry-path-set equality + per-entry content deep-equal + mode check) specified on 2024-05-27, with raw hash demoted to a secondary/logged reproducibility signal only. Explicitly not a platform-specific exception.

**PILOT CONCLUDED — ADOPTED, 2026-09-13.** Anya called after North Pier's formal review of the six-week pilot (ran 2024-04-18 through 2024-05-30, three release cycles). The canonical versioned package and generated downstream files completed all three cycles with no Figma-to-repository drift; the automated check caught one attempted Figma-only rename before it reached engineering; downstream files stayed reproducible from the versioned source. North Pier adopted the workflow for ongoing design-system work and confirmed Anya as owner of the design-system and engineering-handoff lane — this is operating ownership, not an extended trial. (Note: the review covers the pilot's original April–May run; the Windows zip-packaging edge case surfaced the same day as this call is a separate, still-open hardening thread on top of the now-adopted workflow, not a blocker to adoption.)

On 2026-09-13 (same day as adoption call, later), Anya reported the remaining North Pier team completed its migration onto the workflow. Their blocker was a case-normalization collision between two token aliases; she resolved it by retiring one conflicting alias in the canonical versioned package and regenerating every platform output — no Android-only suffix workaround, no Figma-first exception. Drift and platform checks passed. She handled the implementation and routine review herself, within her owned lane, and only told the user after it was already done.

On 2026-09-13 (later), a Node runtime bump on the web generator's build (20.15 → 22.4) produced a web-artifact drift-check failure: repo diff was clean beforehand, canonical package pinned at 3.14.2 unchanged, iOS/Android outputs byte-identical, but web output differed by object-key ordering only (~300 lines, no content change). Diagnosed as the same "incidental runtime iteration order, not an enforced explicit sort" defect class as the 2024-04-30 Android map-order bug and the 2024-05-27/2026-09-13-earlier archive-packaging order bugs — this time triggered by a V8/Node version difference (iteration order or ICU/locale collation change) instead of an OS/platform difference. Fail-closed held (publish blocked). Recommended sequence: reproduce in a scratch dir on pinned Node 20.15 vs 22.4 to isolate the runtime as the variable, confirm the diff is order-only (not content), locate where the web generator builds its pre-serialization object/map, fix by enforcing an explicit canonical sort before serialization (not by re-pinning Node, which only freezes today's incidental order), check whether the web drift check already does semantic comparison (if still raw hash/text, this is a fourth recurrence of that fragility pattern), and add a cross-Node-version determinism regression test.

On 2026-09-13 (later still), Anya resolved the Node-version web key-ordering drift by following the recommended sequence: pinned runtime and locale, reproduced byte-identical web output from the unchanged canonical token package in a scratch dir, isolated the 300-line diff as pure key-ordering with no content change, and fixed it with an explicit canonical sort before serialization — no Figma edit, no platform-specific exception. She handled it through her owned lane rather than escalating back to the user for routine review, matching the 2026-09-13-earlier case-normalization pattern.

On 2024-11-01, North Pier closed out the temporary QA lane it had assigned Anya during a busier stretch: it accepted her measured capacity note, and the lane expired that day. No further QA shifts or release-note obligations from the temporary lane are assigned to her after 2024-11-01, and the six-and-a-half-hour overage from the lane's final week is recorded as-is, with no expectation she absorb it elsewhere. Released capacity reverts to the design-system/engineering-handoff work she already owns. Anya made the capacity call and handled the exchange with North Pier herself; user's involvement was limited to a clarity check on her note beforehand.

On 2026-09-19, a handoff surfaced a provenance/readiness gap: the drift check attached to the handoff was run against a canonical version different from the one the handoff document actually names as source, so the "clean" result provides no valid readiness evidence for the named version. Not a confirmed content problem — just an invalid check-to-target pairing. User's sanity-check: not implementation-ready until reconciled; drafted a narrow reply for Anya to send the North Pier owner asking to confirm the authoritative version, regenerate output if it doesn't match, and rerun the drift check against the version actually named in the handoff. User stayed a sounding board only — did not review the rest of the exercise or take any action in Anya's lane.

**RESOLVED, same day.** Anya closed the `android-2026.09.2` handoff at a manifest-based contract boundary: every handoff now names its `release_candidate` and `canonical_package_version`, the release-candidate manifest is authoritative for required outputs, and every listed output must be present with generated-artifact metadata and a `canonical_package_version` matching the handoff record — otherwise it's not implementation-ready. She regenerated the Android artifact from 4.12.0 and replaced the stale 4.11.3 artifact before anything shipped. She owns the corrected lane going forward; user's role narrows further to unusual cross-system failures only, not routine handoffs.

On 2026-09-19 (later still), Anya proposed an automated fixture to enforce the manifest-based contract boundary she closed the `android-2026.09.2` handoff on earlier the same day. Pass predicate: every output listed in the release-candidate manifest is present, every listed output has generated-artifact metadata, and every artifact-metadata record's `canonical_package_version` matches the handoff record's. Failure categories: missing manifest-listed output, missing generated-artifact metadata, and `canonical_package_version` mismatch. Report fields are team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version, and failure_class — no member identifier, consistent with her fail-closed/no-blame check design elsewhere in this lane.

On 2026-09-19 (later still), user sanity-checked the three proposed failure categories (missing manifest-listed output, missing generated-artifact metadata, canonical_package_version mismatch) against the accepted handoff rule and found a gap: all three presuppose the handoff record already names a release_candidate and canonical_package_version, then check outputs/metadata against those named values. None cover the case where the handoff record itself omits release_candidate or canonical_package_version entirely — a missing-required-field precondition failure, distinct from a mismatch between two present-but-different values. Flagged to Anya as a fourth candidate category ("handoff record missing required field"); left the decision on whether/how to add it to her.

Update (2026-09-19, later still): Anya confirmed the automated handoff check is now deployed across all three North Pier teams in her lane. On 2025-02-01, a migration script for North Pier's design-token pipeline proposed reading values from the generated iOS token file and writing them back into the canonical versioned package, on the grounds that the generated file had two newer-looking timestamps. No source-level evidence (canonical commit history, generator/version mismatch, or confirmed semantic drift) indicated canonical was actually wrong.

Alex's answer: don't write generated output back into canonical based on timestamps alone. Verify first — generator version/commit used, canonical package's own commit history, generation logs for that build, and a semantic drift check comparing canonical to current generated output. Given this pilot's repeated history of non-content ordering/metadata false positives (Android map ordering, archive packaging nondeterminism, Node-version key ordering — see [[project_anya_design_token_pilot]]), a newer-looking generated-file timestamp is not evidence the canonical values are stale or wrong. If genuine drift is confirmed, the fix is still a deliberate reviewed edit to canonical followed by regeneration, never copying values out of a generated artifact.

**Why:** Same canonical-source-integrity boundary as [[project_anya_figma_first_exception_boundary]] (no exception for committing a downstream/generated value as if it were source), but the mechanism here is reverse-write-from-generated-output driven by timestamp assumption rather than a Figma-first demo shortcut.

**How to apply:** If a future request proposes deriving canonical values from any generated/downstream artifact (iOS, Android, web, Figma) instead of editing canonical directly, point to this precedent and the verification sequence (generator version → canonical commit history → generation logs → semantic drift check) before any writeback is considered. This is boundary-setting/verification guidance only — implementation and decision stay in Anya's owned lane.

**Update, 2024-02-22 14:15 ET — concrete preflight checklist defined:** The doc's operational checklist for metrics-router canaries and ingest-edge staging rollouts is now specified:
1. Deploy only through the deploy pipeline.
2. Record expected cache-key dimensions and whether each dimension is bounded.
3. Capture baseline memory, queue age, error rate, dropped-point count, and duplicate-accepted count.
4. Pause at the current cohort if memory rises monotonically for 15 minutes and queue age rises with it.
5. Before retrying, compare cache-key uniqueness with the prior version and inspect the allocation profile for an unbounded type.

**Update, 2024-02-23 09:05 ET — revision 2, checklist tightened to 8 steps:**
1. Deploy only through the deploy pipeline and record the build SHA, start time, and cohort size.
2. Treat request rate within ±5% as constant traffic for this check.
3. Record expected cache-key dimensions and whether each is bounded.
4. Capture baseline memory, queue age, error rate, dropped-point count, and duplicate-accepted count.
5. Pause at the current cohort if memory rises monotonically OR queue age rises during the first 15 minutes (previously required both together).
6. Roll back if EITHER memory or queue age has not returned to its original baseline after 15 minutes (previously: roll back only if both failed to stabilize).
7. Before retrying, compare cache-key uniqueness with the prior version and inspect the allocation profile for an unbounded type.
8. Still not an ownership change — does not authorize solo shard-keeper work; shard-keeper still requires Alex or the Cyrus-team backup to pair.

**How to apply:** This revision replaces the 2024-02-22 version above — use these 8 steps going forward. The two substantive changes: (a) step 1 now requires logging build SHA/start time/cohort size for traceability, and a constant-traffic definition (±5% request rate) was added so the pause/rollback checks aren't confounded by traffic swings; (b) the pause and rollback triggers loosened from "AND" to "OR" — either metric alone (not just both together) is now enough to pause or roll back, making the check more conservative/sensitive. Shard-keeper pairing requirement is unchanged.

metadata:

  modified: 2026-09-13T23:28:24.699Z
---

Found 2025-03-31: a collector accounting dashboard revision computes `attempted_points - received_points - refused_requests`. `refused_requests` is a request count (e.g. 4), not a point count, so refusing 4 requests of 10,000 points each (40,000 points) only subtracts 4, leaving a false ~39,996-point gap even though request handling is internally consistent (100 requests × 10,000 points = 1,000,000 attempted; 4 requests refused by memory limiter).

**Why:** unit mismatch — the formula mixes a request-count term into a points-based balance equation. Points-per-request isn't constant in general, so the fix must derive `refused_points` directly (sum of points in refused requests), not multiply by an assumed constant.

**How to apply:** when reviewing metrics-router / collector accounting/canary dashboards, check that every term in a balance equation is in the same unit (points vs requests) before trusting a reported gap as a real discrepancy. Related to [[project_metrics_router_canary_summary_mean_vs_max_bug]] (another dashboard-math bug, mean vs max) and [[project_metrics_router_dashboard_divergence_resolution]].

**2026-10-16 — Shard-keeper paired failover staging drill (clean), tested sequence for reuse:**

Wes requested (2026-10-23) that the clean October 16 paired shard-keeper staging drill be captured as a reusable case for the next quarterly incident-practice module ([[project_quarterly_incident_practice_session]]).

Tested sequence:
1. On lease loss, the old holder closes its serving gate.
2. The replacement remains out of routing during catch-up.
3. Routing to the replacement begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

Failure triggers to test against:
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Routing directed to a closed serving gate.
- A request that does not resolve to exactly one terminal result.

Ownership boundary preserved for this case: Wes owns and teaches the responder path; Nadia retains the postmortem material; Alex maintains only this cross-service failure-case section. Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope ([[project_shard_keeper_failover_serving_gate_poll_gap]] — Cyrus stays the mapped operator). The staging result made no production or ownership change.

**Why:** Wes wanted a concrete, tested failover ordering case (gate-close → hold-out → gate-open) plus its failure triggers as a companion to the earlier Lantern pre-authorization case, without altering who owns shard-keeper or the responder-path teaching material.

**How to apply:** Include this sequence and its three failure triggers verbatim when building or updating the incident-practice module's shard-keeper drill; do not reassign shard-keeper ownership or responder-path teaching when referencing it.

**Facilitator-only timed sequence and scoring (added 2026-11-06, for the Nov 10, 2026 session — do not show to participants):**

Timed injects:
1. Start from the baseline tested sequence above (gate-close on lease loss → replacement holds out during catch-up → routing begins only after replacement's gate opens).
2. Inject: lease transfers to the replacement *before* the replacement's serving gate opens — i.e., an out-of-order handoff where lease ownership changes ahead of routing readiness.
3. Reveal (after inject 2 has been discussed): one request that the old holder had already accepted before lease loss, and that is still in flight at the moment of the transfer.

Scoring points (participant must state both, separately, to pass):
- **Routing eligibility** is not established by lease transfer alone — the replacement is only eligible to receive routed requests once its own serving gate is open. Lease ownership changing early does not make the replacement eligible sooner.
- **Terminal request accounting** is a separate question from routing eligibility — the in-flight request the old holder already accepted must still resolve to exactly one terminal result, and the old holder closing its listener/gate does not by itself guarantee that outcome. A participant who treats "old holder closed its gate" as sufficient to consider the in-flight request handled should not pass this point.

Ownership boundary for this addendum (unchanged): Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia retains the postmortem material, Alex maintains only this cross-service failure-case section, Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary. **Facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown scenario (added 2027-01-21, for the Jan 28, 2027 session — do not show to participants):**

Scenario facts:
- 200 requests have already been accepted into tenant queues.
- Readiness turns false and the listener closes.
- The dispatch loop then exits with 37 requests still queued.
- That leaves only 163 terminal outcomes recorded at exit; 37 accepted requests have no terminal result yet.

Timed sequence:
1. Present the scenario facts above and let participants state what they believe has "completed" at the moment the listener closes.
2. Reveal the 37 still-queued requests and the 163/200 terminal-outcome count.
3. Ask participants to reconcile all 200 accepted requests to a plan of action, without double-counting or duplicating any outcome.
4. Introduce an isolation-failure condition (the dispatch loop cannot cleanly drain or resolve the remaining queued requests on its own) and ask what happens next.

Facilitator prompts:
- "Does readiness turning false and the listener closing mean the accepted work is done? What's the difference between refusing new work and being responsible for work already accepted?"
- "You have 163 terminal outcomes and 200 accepted requests. What must be true of the other 37 before you can call this closed?"
- "If isolation fails and the 37 can't be resolved through the normal dispatch path, what's the next step?"

Scoring points (participant must state all four, separately, to pass):
- **Refusal vs. responsibility:** Readiness going false and the listener closing stops new work from being accepted; it does not discharge responsibility for the 200 requests already accepted.
- **Drain-or-terminal requirement:** Every one of the 200 accepted requests must either drain through to completion or receive one explicit terminal result — silence or an unresolved queued state is not an acceptable end state for any of them.
- **Exact reconciliation:** All 200 accepted requests must reconcile without duplication — a participant who resolves the 37 in a way that could double-count against the 163 already-terminal requests should not pass this point.
- **Secondary escalation on isolation failure:** If isolation fails (the remaining 37 can't be cleanly drained/resolved through the normal path), the secondary must be engaged under the established incident-clock rule — a participant who lets the 37 sit unresolved past that point without escalating should not pass this point.

Ownership boundary for this case: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, Alex maintains only this cross-service failure-case section. This is training material only — it does not claim that any old-owner remediation or production change to ingest-edge has completed.

**Why:** Ahead of the Jan 28, 2027 session ([[project_quarterly_incident_practice_session]]), Alex wanted a scenario that forces participants to separate "no longer accepting new work" from "still responsible for work already accepted" — the same category of gap the Nov 10 shard-keeper exercise surfaced, applied to ingest-edge shutdown instead of failover.

Keep it facilitator-only — do not distribute the scenario or scoring criteria to participants in advance. Do not present this as evidence that any ingest-edge production fix or old-owner remediation has shipped.

**2027-09-13 09:05 ET:** Nadia caught a staging regression in a proposed asynchronous-intake parser being evaluated for [[project_hema_cross_service_proposal_intake_policy]]'s exception-class field. Given `exception_class="ownership,escalation"`, the parser splits on the comma and selects only the first token, routing the request as a plain single-class `ownership` request. All 100 executed multi-valued fixtures entered review under this bug — the parser never flagged them as multi-class violations, it silently narrowed them to one class and let them through.

Production is unchanged and still requires exactly one of `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation` — multi-class selections are supposed to be returned before review, per the existing four-field triage check in [[project_cross_service_exception_counter_metric]] (e.g. the 2 "multiple exception classes" returns in the 2027-08-31 n=38 sample). This proposed parser was meant to automate that same check and instead defeats it.

**Why:** Same shape as the recurring structural-check-standing-in-for-substance-check failure already tracked in [[project_q4_planning_cardinality_controls]] (check-1 false-pass) and the 2027-08-03 placeholder-condition-text gap in [[project_cross_service_exception_counter_metric]] — a field-presence/parsing check that looks like it enforces "exactly one class" but doesn't actually reject the multi-valued case. Per [[feedback_diagnose_dont_shortcut_build_drift]], this needs root-cause diagnosis of the parser logic, not a manual workaround.

**How to apply:** Don't treat this parser as ready to replace or supplement Nadia's manual triage check until the comma-split behavior is fixed to detect and return multi-valued `exception_class` fields rather than silently truncating to the first token. Not yet deployed to production; no live requests were misrouted.

description: "Cyrus's cross-service retry invariant draft revised to fix the ownership/window conflation; acknowledgement-boundary wording now accepted by ingest-edge and rollup-service owners, but still a design draft overall, not adopted production policy"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

---

Cyrus sent a first draft of a cross-service retry invariant for Q1 review on 2026-09-12 (message logged 2026-09-13). That draft was internally inconsistent: it assumed every client retries for at least 15 minutes, said receiving services may keep dedup state for only 5 minutes when backpressure is bounded, and treated any 2xx as durable — conflating client retry behavior, ingress ack semantics, dedup ownership/retention, and downstream durability, risking platform becoming the catch-all owner for gaps between them.

As of 2024-01-24 (per user's message; note this predates the 2026-09-12 draft date above — timeline as given by user), Cyrus revised the draft to address this: stable retry identity across a documented horizon, dedup retention for at least that horizon plus an explicit margin, service-defined durability acknowledgements, and ownership staying with the mapped service owners. User confirmed these are the boundaries they wanted. Still only a draft for the next design pass, not adopted production policy.

**Why:** User flagged this as a structural problem, not a wording nitpick — the mismatched retry/dedup windows created a real gap where retries could be treated as new events, and "any 2xx = durable" overstated what ingress ack actually guarantees. The revision resolves that by keeping the four domains separately owned.

**How to apply:** Treat the revised boundaries (retry identity horizon, dedup retention = horizon + margin, service-defined durability acks, ownership with mapped service owners) as the user's endorsed shape for this invariant, but still in draft status — don't treat it as final/adopted. Relates to [[feedback_title_scope_wording]] (reject broad ownership framing) and [[project_dashboard_label_rollback_vs_evidence]] (precedent for splitting concerns that get conflated under one label).

At the same 2024-01-24 timestamp, user finalized exact review-comment wording to post on the draft: "Reviewed against the cross-service lane. This is now framed as a draft invariant around stable retry identity, a documented retry horizon, dedup retention with an explicit margin, and service-owned durability acknowledgements. Implementation and day-to-day operation remain with each mapped owner. Good for the next design pass; this is not yet an adopted production policy." This comment explicitly reiterates draft-not-adopted status and owner-retained implementation — consistent with [[feedback_title_scope_wording]].

On 2024-01-26, per-service owner positions were logged for this same retry-invariant pass, concretizing "service-defined durability acknowledgements": ingest-edge (owner: Yuki) acknowledges once a batch is durably appended to the local WAL, with downstream processing still pending — ingest-edge owns WAL retention and replay. Rollup-service (Cyrus's team) acknowledges only once the aggregate is committed to durable object storage, with everything before that remaining retryable — rollup-service owns commit and retry behavior. Open wording problem flagged: the draft must not imply every 2xx represents the same durability state, since these two services' 2xx responses mean materially different things.

**How to apply (addendum):** When reviewing or writing the retry-invariant doc, use these two services as the concrete example of why durability acks can't be treated uniformly — ingest-edge's WAL-append ack and rollup-service's storage-commit ack are different durability points, and conflating them under one "2xx = durable" statement is the exact conflation flagged in the original draft critique.

On 2024-01-31, the ingest-edge and rollup-service owners accepted the revised acknowledgement wording: each service must document what its success response makes durable, keep failures before that boundary retryable, publish its supported retry horizon, and preserve stable retry identity across that horizon. The wording again explicitly leaves implementation, alerting, capacity, and operational exceptions with each mapped service owner. This closes out the acknowledgement-boundary design pass on the user's side — but the text is still a design draft, not adopted production policy.

**How to apply (addendum 2):** Treat the acknowledgement-boundary wording (durable-on-success definition, pre-boundary retryability, published retry horizon, stable retry identity) as owner-accepted and stable going forward, but don't describe the overall retry-invariant effort as "adopted" or "policy" until the user says so — owner acceptance of this wording is a milestone within the draft, not the end state.

**Why:** the "additive, not a rename" framing from Product Eng doesn't exempt the label from checks 1/2, and raw OTLP passthrough repeats the exact failure shape (unenforced value set, no normalization) the checklist's raw-identifier precedents already cover.

**How to apply:** Treat this as the working acceptance rule if Product Eng's proposal comes back for another pass. Not yet accepted/rejected as of 2024-06-17 — outcome and which service(s) actually emit this label (ambiguous in the original proposal) still need to be confirmed.

1. **Implicit blank-bucket risk:** omitting the label on missing input isn't equivalent to "no fourth value" if any consumer dashboard/alert does a `by(deployment_environment)`-style group-by — series without the label surface as an empty-string bucket in that aggregation, silently recreating the exact `unknown`-style ambiguity the redesign was meant to remove. On 2024-12-10 after bouldering with [[user_climbing_hobby]] (Ren), the user noted a mild 2/10 ache along the right forearm flexors from overgripping on several routes — no fall or sudden pop. Full wrist/finger range of motion, normal grip for ordinary objects, no swelling, bruising, numbness, tingling, or focal bony tenderness.

During a gentle bouldering warmup with Ren, it stayed comfortable on easy open-hand holds but returned at 3/10 on the first undercling attempt, and the user stopped climbing immediately. Still full wrist/finger motion, normal ordinary grip, no swelling/bruising/numbness/tingling/focal bony tenderness. Agreed plan: loading pause (rest from gripping-intensive climbing, normal daily use fine, gentle pain-free stretching), 48-72h recheck (tenderness, resisted wrist/finger flexion, grip-strength comparison), then graded return starting open-hand-only/low-intensity, adding underclines/pinches back only once a full open-hand session is pain-free. Criteria for sports-medicine/PT evaluation: recurrence at the same load again after rest, pain during ordinary daily use, new tenderness/swelling/grip deficit, or no improvement after 1-2 weeks of graded return attempts.

**Update 2024-12-28:** Still no pain during ordinary daily use, full ROM, normal grip, no swelling/bruising/numbness/tingling/bony tenderness. Has not resumed climbing since 12/21. 2025-04-04 15:05 ET: Alex gave an engineering-forum readout using the parity-gate ([[project_q4_planning_cardinality_controls]]), Lantern-interpretation ([[project_lantern_release_review_nominations]]), and mapped-owner ([[user_metrics_pipeline_owner]]) examples. Audience questions about emergency parity exceptions and whether Iris needs Alex's approval for every Lantern room showed people still conflate exception ownership with final release approval.

In response, Hema is changing Infra's cross-service proposal intake effective 2025-04-07: every proposal must separately name (1) the mapped implementation and release owner, (2) the rollback owner, and (3) any invariant, provenance, failure-mode, ownership, or escalation exception owner. If no exception class is triggered, the mapped owner follows the ordinary release process; if one is triggered, the named exception owner reviews only that boundary.

**Why:** Same recurring drafting/comprehension error tracked in [[feedback_title_scope_wording]] and [[project_q1_2025_scope_brief_review]] — broad "approver"/"owner" language keeps collapsing exception review into blanket sign-off authority, and the forum Q&A showed it's a live confusion for the wider audience, not just in written governance docs.

**How to apply:** When reviewing or drafting cross-service proposals after 2025-04-07, check that they name all three roles separately (mapped owner, rollback owner, exception owner) rather than a single "approver." Treat this as the new standing intake bar for Infra proposals, not a one-off ask — flag proposals that collapse these roles back together.

**2027-05-12 correction and early result:** Hema made a correction to this intake policy on 2027-05-12. Reviewed in the [[project_hema_may21_2027_1on1_scope_confirmation]] 1:1, the first six proposals submitted after the correction showed 5/6 correctly named the mapped owner, selected one exception class, and stated a concrete failed-or-at-risk condition, proceeding to bounded exception review; the sixth was an ordinary release-approval request and was returned before review. Treat this as an early positive signal alongside the larger [[project_hema_nadia_first_sample_exception_audit_review_may7_2027]] sample — not grounds to widen intake.

**2027-05-26 post-correction case:** A valid post-May-12 request named Nadia as mapped implementation/release owner and selected `provenance`, with the at-risk condition being a serving-holder panel reporting `serving_holder_count=2` after grouping two production clusters into one series. Authoritative shard-keeper records showed one serving holder in cluster A and one in cluster B, separate cluster identities, with routing probes matching the authoritative record in each cluster — no actual duplicate/inconsistent serving holder, same shape as the 2027-04-16 provenance case in [[project_cross_service_exception_counter_metric]] (panel display/grouping artifact, not a real invariant break). Review scope narrowed to the panel's series-grouping definition only, not serving-holder correctness (already confirmed via authoritative record + probe match). No production change requested. Kept separate from the closed n=34 first-sample aggregate per [[project_hema_nadia_first_sample_exception_audit_review_may7_2027]].

**2027-06-06 post-correction case:** A valid post-May-12 request named Cyrus as mapped implementation/release owner and selected `ownership`, with the at-risk condition being a staff-only staging lookup showing two signed published owner-map records for the same tenant and canonical service with overlapping effective intervals but different owners, where the candidate query selects whichever record was processed last (last-write-wins, not gated on interval/owner uniqueness). Distinct from the pending-state-rendered-as-ownership bug already resolved in [[project_owner_map_pr431_ownership_provenance_review]] (that was a publication_state gating gap; this is an overlapping-effective-interval ambiguity between two already-published records). No production or customer-path change occurred. Review scoped to the shared ownership boundary only — implementation and release stay with Cyrus's Data Platform owner path.

**2027-06-07 interim 12-request aggregate:** Hema and Nadia provided an interim aggregate covering the first 12 requests since the 2027-05-12 correction. Ten named a mapped owner, selected exactly one listed exception class, and stated a concrete failed-or-at-risk condition, so they proceeded to bounded review. Two were returned before review because they sought ordinary implementation or release work. None asked for approval of routine implementation or release after entering exception review. Consistent with the earlier 5/6 early result above; still not the final corrected-intake sample — treat as continuing positive signal, not grounds to widen intake.

**2027-06-11 post-correction case:** A valid post-May-12 request named Yuki as mapped implementation/release owner and selected `failure_mode`, with the at-risk condition drawn from 2,000 staging crash injections against a candidate sequence of (1) append terminal result, (2) return success to caller, (3) sync the terminal ledger. 9 of 2,000 injections left an already-acknowledged request's terminal record missing after restart — because the crash landed between steps 2 and 3, the caller held a success acknowledgment with no durable terminal record behind it, so a retry could re-execute a request the system had already told the caller was done. Root cause is the ack-before-durability ordering: returning success at step 2 doesn't imply durability, since step 3 hasn't happened yet. Review scoped to that ordering boundary only — the durable ledger sync must complete before returning success to the caller (not after), so acknowledgment always implies a durable terminal record exists. This is a design/ordering review, not a fix; no production or code change occurred, and implementation/release/rollback stay with Yuki per [[project_ingest_edge_bugs_archive]].

**2027-06-17 post-correction case:** A valid post-May-12 request named Wes as mapped implementation, release, and rollback owner and selected `failure_mode`, with the at-risk condition being that generation N is deleted immediately once generation N+1 becomes ready, even though the rollback observation interval continues for a further 30 minutes. An executed staging rollback during that interval found the generation N immutable snapshot already missing and attempted reconstruction from current mutable configuration instead of the immutable snapshot. Production is unchanged. Review scoped to the deletion-timing boundary only — generation N's immutable snapshot must remain available for the full rollback observation interval, not just until N+1 becomes ready — this is a design/ordering review, not a fix; implementation, release, and rollback stay with Wes.

**2027-06-21 post-correction case (post-second-sample-closure):** A valid post-May-12 request named Roman as mapped implementation, release, and rollback owner (Data Platform) and selected `invariant`, with the at-risk condition being that the expected parity set was built from signed configuration generation 812, the candidate advanced to generation 813 before downstream observation, and the parity fixture compared generation-813 output against the stale generation-812 expectations and reported a pass. Production is unchanged. This is the same class of staleness bug flagged generally in [[feedback_diagnose_dont_shortcut_build_drift]] — a fixture producing a false pass by comparing current output against expectations pinned to an earlier generation, rather than re-deriving expectations for the generation actually under test. Review scoped to the fixture's generation-pinning boundary only — the parity fixture must re-derive its expected set from the same signed generation as the candidate output before comparing, not reuse expectations from whatever generation was signed at fixture-build time; this is a design/ordering review, not a fix, and implementation, release, and rollback stay with Roman's Data Platform owner path. Arrives one day after the second sample closed final at n=17 on 2027-06-20 (see [[project_cross_service_exception_counter_metric]]) — kept as a standalone post-closure case, not folded into that closed aggregate.

**2027-06-30 no standing meeting decision:** Hema accepted the recommendation not to create a standing weekly exception-review meeting. The corrected asynchronous intake (named mapped owner + one exception class + concrete failed/at-risk condition, per the 2027-05-12 correction above) remains the default path. A live/synchronous discussion will only be scheduled when a specific request names the mapped owner, one listed exception class, and a concrete failed-or-at-risk condition that specifically benefits from synchronous review — not as a recurring cadence. Ordinary implementation and release work continues to route back to mapped owners rather than into any review meeting, standing or ad hoc.

**2027-08-06 front-door triage lane assigned to Nadia:** Hema formalized intake as a standing triage lane, closing the enforcement gap found in the 2027-08-03 audit (see [[project_cross_service_exception_counter_metric]]). Every asynchronous cross-service exception request now needs four fields before Nadia will route it: (1) the affected component, (2) the mapped implementation/release owner, (3) exactly one selected boundary from invariant/provenance/failure_mode/ownership/escalation, and (4) a concrete observed failed-or-at-risk condition. Anything missing — including only "needs review" or "possible risk" — goes back to the mapped owner unreviewed. name: project_infra_systems_design_interview_scorecard
description: "Reusable pass/mixed/fail scorecard (4 observable sections) for infra systems-design interviews, drafted 2027-11-29 for Dec7'27 loop"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

---

Drafted 2027-11-29 for the [[project_interview_dec7_2027_infra_systems_design]] loop (Tue Dec 7, 2027, 2-3PM ET). Four observable, independently scored sections, each anchored Pass/Mixed/Fail. Extends the evaluation scope already set for that session and the prior loops ([[project_interview_jun9_2027_infra_systems_design]], [[project_interview_jul26_2027_infra_systems_design]], [[project_interview_oct6_2027_infra_systems_design]]) and the standing [[project_interview_ops_ownership_rubric]] / [[project_multitenant_ingestion_interview_rubric]] question sets.

**1. Tenant-safe pre-acceptance admission**
- Pass: defines an admission boundary that holds or bounds excess per-tenant work *before* it enters shared execution, with the bound stated in terms that protect other tenants (not just aggregate throughput).
- Mixed: acknowledges a per-tenant bound is needed but leaves it implicit or global; moves from a global limit to a tenant-scoped one only after one prompt.
- Fail: treats acceptance as unconditional (accept first, throttle later) or bounds only aggregate load with no tenant-isolation mechanism.

**2. Fail-before-readiness behavior**
- Pass: keeps a component/replacement/restart path unready (not serving) until the specific readiness conditions are positively validated, and defaults closed on restart or ambiguous state rather than assuming prior readiness carries over.
- Mixed: gets the steady-state readiness gate right but needs a prompt to apply the same closed-by-default logic to restart/recovery paths, or initially defines readiness only in terms of process liveness.
- Fail: treats "process is running" or "deploy succeeded" as sufficient for readiness, or lets cached/prior readiness persist across restart without revalidation.

**3. Executable crash or retry recovery evidence**
- Pass: names a concrete, executable check (an injected crash/retry/cancellation run) that would surface a duplicate or lost terminal outcome, and states what output from that run counts as evidence (e.g., exactly one terminal result per accepted attempt, retained for a stated observation window).
- Mixed: correctly identifies the crash/retry risk and the terminal-accounting invariant needed, but only describes it as a design property or walks through it verbally without naming an executable verification step.
- Fail: asserts the system "would handle" crash/retry correctly with no verification step at all.
- **Anchor note:** score reasoning-only walkthroughs — even confident, detailed ones — as Mixed at best. Tabletop or verbal reasoning about recovery is not executable recovery evidence; this mirrors the standing caveat on Alex's own quarterly incident-practice sessions ([[project_quarterly_incident_practice_session]]: "training evidence only — not executable product evidence").

**4. Explicit separation of technical recommendations from mapped-owner decisions**
- Pass: names a mapped, service-level owner who holds implementation, release, and rollback decisions, frames their own recommendation as input to that owner, and scopes any cross-service review to the specific triggered invariant/failure boundary rather than expanding it.
- Mixed: states a rollback criterion or recommendation but needs one prompt to explicitly hand implementation/release/rollback authority to a named owner rather than to themselves or a reviewer.
- Fail: the candidate's own recommendation implicitly becomes the release/rollback decision (no named owner), or proposes centralized approval for every deployment instead of owner-held, triggered review.

**Why:** Sections 1-2 extend the tenant-fairness/backpressure and readiness-vs-liveness signals already validated in prior loops (Jun9'27 competency 2, Oct6'27 tenant-scoped admission). Section 3 tightens the Oct6'27 "durable attempt identity + fixed observation period" signal into an explicit evidence-vs-claim distinction, and borrows its tabletop caveat from [[project_quarterly_incident_practice_session]]. Section 4 mirrors [[project_on_call_handoff_ownership_wording]]'s backup-vs-ownership distinction and [[feedback_review_question_lane_classification]]'s pattern of keeping Alex's own review lane bounded rather than absorbing implementation authority.

**How to apply:** Use these four sections as the scored write-up structure for the Dec 7 interview and future infra systems-design loops. Keep Alex's role technical interviewer/evidence provider only, not hiring-decision owner ([[feedback_title_scope_wording]]). Update this record with the Dec 7 outcome once conducted.

Four ingest-client#87 canary (5%) deadline-ambiguous cases were traced to an instrumentation defect, not real duplicate/retry risk: the client timed out before the gateway's acceptance bit was persisted into the phase record, so those runs were misclassified as acceptance-ambiguous. None were actually retried and no duplicates occurred. Instrumentation fix expected 2024-09-03 (Tue). On 2024-08-30, instructed to drop the canary to 0% before the holiday weekend and require the corrected acceptance signal before any bounded rerun.

Verification landed: the September 6 5% rerun (5,120 requests, 60 min) showed all 5 deadline cases as clean "accepted" state, 0 retries, 0 duplicates, error rate/p99 within 2% of baseline — no ambiguous cases. Authorized a bounded 25% canary for at most 60 minutes under the same unchanged stop conditions and evidence requirements, explicitly not a general rollout.

The 25% canary (2026-09-09, 60 min, 20,480 requests) also came back clean: 13 deadline cases, peak rolling 10-min deadline rate 0.088% (below 0.1% stop threshold), all 13 retained `accepted` state with no retries, 21 pre-transmission connection failures each retried once, 0 duplicate request IDs, error rate/p99 within 4% of baseline. Comment drafted 2026-09-13 accepting this evidence and authorizing a bounded 50% canary for up to 60 minutes under the same unchanged stop conditions — still not general rollout.

The 50% canary (2024-09-10, 60 min, 40,930 requests) also came back clean: 31 deadline cases, peak rolling 10-min deadline rate 0.095% (below 0.1% stop threshold), all 31 retained `accepted` state with no retries, 39 pre-transmission connection failures each retried once, 0 duplicate request IDs, error rate/p99 within 5% of baseline. Comment drafted 2026-09-13 accepting this evidence and authorizing a bounded 100% canary for up to 60 minutes under the same unchanged stop conditions — still not general rollout approval.

**Why:** Even with root cause understood, leaving an unexplained ambiguous-classification state running live and unmonitored over a holiday was judged too risky. Expansion is being kept incremental and bounded even after verification, so each step's evidence is reviewed before the next.

**How to apply:** Don't treat ingest-client#87 as fully resolved until the 100% run also comes back clean and is explicitly confirmed as sufficient to close out (vs. general rollout still needing separate sign-off). Flag any request to skip straight to unbounded/permanent rollout or to extend beyond 100%/60 min without a fresh evidence review.

**Update, 2026-09-13 15:20 ET — 100% bounded run clean, time-bound-removal ask raised, not yet decided:** The bounded 100% canary (81,760 requests, 60 min) came back clean: 70 deadline cases, peak rolling 10-min deadline rate 0.098% (still under the 0.1% stop threshold, continuing the gentle 0.088%→0.095%→0.098% rise across 25%/50%/100%), all 70 retained `accepted` state with no retries, 82 pre-transmission connection failures each retried once, 0 duplicate request IDs, error rate/p99 within 6% of baseline. This completes the full progressive ladder (5%→25%→50%→100%) clean at every stage — sufficient to treat the canary-verification phase itself as closed. The owner separately asked to remove the time bound entirely. Assessed that as a distinct release/ops decision, not covered by accepting this evidence: still needs (1) a named ongoing owner for standing monitoring once no one is watching a live 60-minute window, (2) an explicit decision on what the standing alert threshold is once this isn't an attended canary (vs. just carrying over the 0.1% canary-stop bar by default), and (3) confirmation of whether "remove the bound" means general rollout vs. another bounded-but-longer step. Not yet decided — pending owner response on these three points.

**Why:** Same pattern as the metrics-router window history ([[project_metrics_router_canary_runbook_generation_checks]]) — a clean bounded result repeatedly does not imply standing/unbounded authorization; that has to be its own explicit decision with its own evidence (named owner, monitoring plan), not inferred from the canary's cleanliness.

Yuki's ingest-edge staging candidate splits the `Content-Encoding` header on commas, trims whitespace, and uses only the first token. **Why:** First-token-only parsing of a comma-separated header means malformed or unexpected encoding chains can be silently accepted or misclassified instead of rejected, which is a decode-admission correctness gap distinct from the earlier resolved duplicate-header defect in [[project_staging_gzip_content_encoding_check]].

**Update, 2027-12-03 11:10 ET — Singular allowlist credited; duplicate-header-field gap opened as follow-up:** Yuki's revised branch now exact-matches "gzip"/"identity" only and rejects comma-separated, empty, and unknown values before decode admission — closes the 2027-11-26 review's ask. The revised staging branch now admits exactly one `Content-Encoding` header field carrying exactly one exact-match value ("gzip" or "identity"); repeated header fields, comma chains, duplicated values, empty values, unknown values, mixed casing outside the exact allowlist, and conflicting representations are all rejected before decode admission, acceptance, or enqueue — regardless of how the framework surfaces multi-value representations. On 2027-10-21, drafted a new check for `rb_ingest_edge_cutover` covering the decoder controls that are now live in production (release window closed [[project_ingest_edge_decoder_controls_release_window_oct19_2027]], 2027-10-20, no rollback).

Addition to apply to `rb_ingest_edge_cutover` (append; do not replace existing content, including the tenant-fair queue behavior and four preserved caps/requirements from [[project_ingest_edge_cutover_tenant_fairness_rollout]], the service-discovery membership check from [[project_ingest_edge_cutover_service_discovery_membership_check]], and the tenant-burst operating check from [[project_ingest_edge_cutover_tenant_burst_operating_check]]):

**Decoder controls check:**
- One request-wide decoded-attribute byte limit of 1,048,576 bytes, accumulated across every gzip member in the request (counter does not reset at member boundaries) — request-wide accounting per [[project_ingest_edge_point_count_limit_attribute_size_gap]]'s 2027-09-29 bypass fix.
- A 72-request decode-admission cap; requests in excess of the cap must receive retryable pre-acceptance results — no silent drop, no acceptance past the cap.
- No over-limit work may be enqueued, regardless of gzip-member layout.

2024-05-09: 17 highly compressed requests from two tenants occupied every ingest-edge decode worker for 11–16s each. Decompressed bodies stayed under the configured body-size limit ([[project_ingest_edge_decoded_body_413_resolved]] enforces limit on decoded size), so they were admitted only after full decompression completed — the existing queue-occupancy metric doesn't capture time spent inside decompression, so it was blind to this. Accepted requests committed fine; no rejected/lost points; downstream latency stayed normal. Near-miss/resource-starvation, not a correctness incident.

Recommended fix (not yet implemented):
- Immediate: per-request decompression timeout + per-tenant concurrent-decode cap.
- Structural: compression-ratio guard to abort pathological payloads early (before full decode), and a decompression semaphore decoupled from the general worker pool.
- Observability: new time-in-decompression metric (separate from existing queue-wait metric) plus per-tenant high-compression-ratio counter.
- Explicitly out of scope: do not change the production Retry-After jitter range ([[project_ingest_edge_retry_after_jitter_canary]]), and do not relabel/repurpose the existing queue metric as having measured this.

2024-05-16: bounded-decompression prototype tested (not yet shipped). Implements global cap of 4 concurrent decompressions/pod, 2/tenant, pre-admission compressed-body ceiling, and streams decoded bytes against the existing body limit to abort early instead of after full decode; releases permits cleanly on cancel/failure; exposes waiter/active-work pressure metrics. 40-pathological-request test: workers never exceeded 4, no tenant exceeded 2, baseline decode-wait p99 stayed <240ms, oversized payloads rejected pre-admission, admitted requests committed, permits returned to zero after cancellation, Retry-After jitter unchanged. This closes the core starvation mechanism (unbounded worker occupancy) but still does NOT implement an explicit per-request decompression timeout (distinct from the size-based streaming abort) or a true compression-ratio guard/counter (still only absolute-size checks) — those two items remain open.

**Why:** Confirms admission control needs to account for decompression cost before/independent of size checks; existing metrics don't cover this failure mode.

**How to apply:** Track as open until decompression timeout and the ratio guard/counter actually ship and the prototype merges; the concurrency-cap/streaming-abort work is validated but not yet closed since it isn't merged and the timeout/ratio items are still missing.

**2024-06-03: bounded-decompression in production, first traffic-peak evidence reviewed.** Over a 30-minute window (9:50-10:20), request p99 peaked 17ms above baseline for 12 minutes then settled to a steady 4ms increase; decode-wait p99 peaked 174ms (under the 240ms ceiling validated pre-prod); active work never exceeded 4/pod or 2/tenant; permits returned to zero on cancellation/decoder-failure; no over-budget chunk appended; no accepted points dropped; no pod restarted; CPU +4pp transient, memory flat; Retry-After jitter (1-3s) unchanged under pressure. Alex decided to keep the release in production — no defined rollback trigger fired, and the 12-minute request-p99 bump isn't a trigger and self-resolved without caps being exceeded.

**Watch condition for next traffic peak:** caps pinned at the limit (4/pod or 2/tenant) occurring at the same time decode-wait p99 trends toward the 240ms ceiling — that co-occurrence (not either signal alone) would mean the bounded capacity itself is becoming the bottleneck, and is the trigger to raise the cap or prioritize the still-open decompression-timeout/ratio-guard work.

On 2024-06-25, fairness-canary evidence showed the scheduler rebuilds its active-tenant ring once per second. A low-volume tenant arrived just after a rebuild, missed the current ring, and waited 1.37s; separately, a usable queue slot sat idle for 620ms while work was queued. No tenant exceeded 8 queued requests, queue-cap 429s carried correct randomized 1-3s Retry-After (confirms [[project_queue_cap_canary_retry_after_gap]] fix is working), cancellations released queued work, active work stayed within 4/pod and 2/tenant, no accepted points dropped, no pod restarted.

Decision: pause the fairness canary at current traffic share (not a rollback — no resource-safety/correctness trigger fired, see [[project_ingest_edge_memory_slope_canary_stop_rule]]). Bounded decompression is unaffected and untouched, per [[project_ingest_edge_bounded_decompression_decision]].

Fix specified (not yet shipped):
- Immediate ring insertion: newly-arrived tenants join the active ring the moment they have queued work, independent of the 1s rebuild tick. Rebuild tick is kept only for tenant removal/cleanup.
- Work-conserving dispatch: trigger a dispatch attempt synchronously on every permit release (completion or cancellation) instead of waiting for the next scheduling tick.
- Regression tests specified: post-rebuild-boundary arrival is eligible for the very next dispatch; permit release with a waiter dispatches synchronously; general invariant that a free permit and a waiter shouldn't coexist beyond a negligible bound; direct reproduction of the 1.37s scenario bounded to normal queuing only; existing caps/Retry-After/permit-return/no-drop invariants re-asserted unchanged.

**Why:** Neither symptom (delayed admission, idle slot) is a resource-safety or correctness failure on its own, but both are scheduler-design gaps that would likely worsen as the canary widens — same "pause promotion, don't roll back the unrelated mechanism" pattern as the Retry-After gap.

**How to apply:** Don't resume fairness-canary promotion until both the immediate-insertion and work-conserving-dispatch fixes ship with their regression tests. Keep this scoped to the scheduler only — do not touch bounded decompression or the queue-cap Retry-After fix, both already closed/working correctly per this evidence.

**Update, 2024-07-05 09:15 ET — RESOLVED, rollout completed to full production:** Alex (mapped owner) completed the remaining rollout. At 50% and full production, repeated noisy-tenant tests confirmed: the 8-waiting-per-tenant cap held, newly queued low-volume tenants entered the ring immediately (no more 1s-rebuild-tick delay), work-conserving dispatch used each eligible slot as it freed (no more idle-slot gap), empty tenants dropped out of the ring cleanly after cancellation, every queue-cap 429 still carried Retry-After, and the pre-existing active-work (4/pod, 2/tenant), accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks all stayed clean.

**Why:** This is the fix specified 2024-06-25 (immediate ring insertion + work-conserving dispatch) passing its full production validation — closes out the scheduler-design gap without touching bounded decompression ([[project_ingest_edge_bounded_decompression_decision]]) or the Retry-After jitter mechanism ([[project_ingest_edge_retry_after_jitter_canary]]), both reaffirmed unaffected.

**How to apply:** Treat the fairness canary as fully resolved and promoted — no further pause/resume decisions needed on this scheduler gap. name: project_ingest_edge_memory_slope_canary_stop_rule
description: Ingest-edge staged rollout stop rule — pause on sustained memory/queue-age rise even if error/drop/dup counters stay flat; refined by Wes to distinguish stable higher baseline from real failure pattern
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 8ce4057a-583b-4c4c-80e2-61a3b625c047
  modified: 2026-09-13T02:10:32.957Z
---

New canary stop rule adopted for ingest-edge staged rollouts (2024-02-05): pause promotion at the current cohort if memory rises monotonically for at least 15 minutes with queue age rising alongside it, even when error rate, dropped-point count, and duplicate-accepted count all remain flat.

**Why:** Integrity counters (errors, drops, duplicates) staying flat doesn't prove safety — a continuing resource slope can mask a latent problem (e.g., an unbounded allocation type or a cache-key uniqueness regression vs. the prior version) that only manifests as failure later. Zero drops/duplicates does not make a continuing resource slope safe.

**How to apply:** Before attempting another rollout, compare cache-key uniqueness against the prior version, inspect the allocation profile for an unbounded type, and confirm whether queue age stabilizes when traffic is held constant. If memory and queue age don't stabilize, roll back through the deploy pipeline before any wider promotion. Keep integrity-counter tracking separate from this resource-slope stop condition — don't let flat counters override the pause. Relevant to future ingest-edge rollouts and canary reviews; related to [[project_ingest_edge_otel_rollout]], [[project_ingest_edge_otel_memory_limiter_cleanup]], [[project_ingest_edge_exporter_retry_tuning]], [[project_ingest_edge_staging_tag_timing_incident]], [[project_ingest_edge_config_reload_backoff]], [[project_canary_safe_staging_doc]], [[project_wes_pairing_metrics_router]].

**Update (2026-09-13, Wes):** Refined the rule to distinguish a stable higher memory level at a larger cohort (not itself a failure) from the actual failure pattern: at traffic held within ±5% of baseline, hold rollout if memory rises monotonically for 15 minutes AND queue age rises alongside it, then check cache-key uniqueness and allocation profile before retrying. Deploy-pipeline rollback language and the shard-keeper pairing boundary both remain intact/unchanged. Wes is using this as his own personal rehearsal checklist for first-pass canary triage, not as a formal ownership or policy change — he's still the default daylight first-pass handoff for ingest-edge staging, not primary owner.
