Yuki's test (2027-07-14) found a single request with a 9 MB attribute string still passes ingest-edge's existing 8,000-point limit, since that rule only counts points, not attribute-string size. 100 concurrent compressed requests each meeting the point-count rule but carrying large attributes raised resident memory from 1.1 GiB to 3.2 GiB before enqueue.

**Why:** The 8,000-point limit is a point-count check, not a payload-size or per-request memory-bound check — it was never designed to cap attribute string size, so it doesn't fail this case even though it's still enforced and working as originally specified.

**How to apply:** This is a gap, not a regression — the point-count limit stays in force unchanged. Treat this as a candidate for a separate attribute-size or per-request payload cap, distinct from [[project_ingest_edge_bounded_decompression_decision]] (which governs decompressed-body size, not attribute-field size). Ingest-edge bugs are tracked in [[project_ingest_edge_bugs_archive]].

**2027-08-05 update:** Yuki's candidate branch adds a 1,048,576-byte aggregate decoded-attribute limit per request (the 8,000-point whole-batch rule is unchanged, separate check). Implementation fully decodes the request into memory first, sums attribute bytes, then rejects over-limit requests before acceptance/enqueue. Executed tests so far: one compressed and one uncompressed request at/above the limit only — no capacity-derivation rationale (why 1,048,576 was chosen) and no concurrent-request test. Since the check runs after full decode, it does not by itself address the pre-enqueue memory spike seen under 100 concurrent compressed requests — a single request could still be decoded fully into memory before the size check fires, so concurrent oversized-but-under-limit-individually or in-flight-during-decode requests could still spike memory. Still untriaged/unmerged as of 2027-08-05.

**2027-08-09 update:** Yuki revised the decoder to count aggregate decoded attribute bytes during streaming (not after full decode) and stop at 1,048,576 bytes before acceptance/enqueue — this addresses the prior full-decode-first concern. Boundary behavior confirmed: gzip and uncompressed requests pass at exactly 1,048,576 bytes, fail at 1,048,577 bytes with zero accepted work. The 8,000-point whole-batch rule remains separate and unchanged. Yuki now ties the proposed bound to a 384 MiB per-instance decoded-request budget (capacity rationale), but still has no representative concurrent-execution test, no resident-memory result under concurrency, and no concurrent terminal-accounting result — so the original 100-concurrent-request memory-spike scenario is still unverified against the fix. Still untriaged/unmerged as of 2027-08-09.

**2027-08-19 update:** First concurrent evidence. Mixed 64 compressed + 64 uncompressed requests at the exact 1,048,576-byte boundary peaked 358 MiB above a 1.12 GiB baseline (within the 384 MiB budget) with one terminal result per request — confirms streaming byte-counting and terminal-accounting hold under concurrency. Limit-plus-one requests still stop before acceptance/enqueue at concurrency; 8,000-point rule unchanged. But a separate 96-request compressed-only burst at the same boundary peaked 451 MiB above baseline, exceeding the 384 MiB budget the bound is meant to enforce — so the per-request limit doesn't yet reconcile to a safe per-instance concurrency/capacity bound under a compression-heavy burst. Alex accepted the streaming/terminal-accounting results but kept the proposed 1,048,576-byte bound blocked pending Yuki reconciling the over-budget compressed burst (either a concurrency/capacity limit on concurrent decodes, or a revised per-request budget derived from worst-case concurrency math). Alex is not implementation/release/rollback owner; Yuki owns the fix and rollback per [[project_ingest_edge_bugs_archive]]. Still open as of 2027-08-19.

**2027-08-30 update:** Yuki's candidate now adds a cap of 72 concurrent boundary-sized decoded requests admitted to decode at once, addressing the over-budget compressed-burst finding above. In an executed 96-request compressed burst: the 72 admitted requests peaked 371 MiB above the 1.12 GiB baseline (within the 384 MiB budget), the 24 excess requests received retryable pre-acceptance results (not enqueued), and every request still received exactly one terminal result — so streaming byte-counting, terminal-accounting, and the concurrency/capacity reconciliation all hold for this burst shape. However, no sustained mixed-size representative workload was supplied, so it's still unverified whether the 72-concurrent-decode cap preserves ordinary accepted throughput under realistic, non-worst-case traffic (as opposed to only under boundary-sized worst-case bursts). Bound remains blocked pending that throughput evidence. Alex sent Yuki a response accepting the pre-acceptance and terminal-accounting correctness of this burst result but keeping the 1,048,576-byte limit and 72-concurrent-decode cap blocked pending sustained/representative-traffic throughput evidence; implementation, release, and rollback remain Yuki's per [[project_ingest_edge_bugs_archive]]. Still open as of 2027-08-30.

**2027-09-02 update:** Yuki ran 2 hours of representative (non-worst-case) traffic against the 1,048,576-byte limit and 72-concurrent-decode cap. Peak memory rose 368 MiB above the 1.12 GiB baseline, within the 384 MiB budget; boundary-sized excess requests were still rejected before acceptance; every admitted request still received exactly one terminal outcome. This closes the sustained-throughput evidence gap from 2027-08-30. New finding: accepted throughput under this representative load was 9.1% below the uncapped baseline and p99 latency was 14% higher — a cost of the cap that wasn't visible in prior worst-case-only bursts. Whether that throughput/latency cost is acceptable is an open question for Yuki (owner) to weigh, not yet resolved. Still open as of 2027-09-02.

**2027-09-08 update:** Yuki made a buffer-reuse change and re-ran a 4-hour sustained representative traffic test (same 1,048,576-byte limit, same 72-concurrent-decode cap). Peak decoded-request memory was 347 MiB above the 1.12 GiB baseline (still within the 384 MiB budget). The throughput/latency cost from 2027-09-02 improved substantially: accepted throughput was only 0.8% below the uncapped baseline (down from 9.1%) and p99 completion time only 2.4% higher (down from 14%). Limit-plus-one and cap-excess work still got retryable pre-acceptance results with no over-limit work enqueued, and every request still had exactly one terminal outcome. Production remains unchanged. This largely resolves the cost-tradeoff concern raised 2027-09-02, pending Alex/Yuki confirming the improved numbers are acceptable to close the gap.

**2027-09-27 update — bypass found:** Yuki found a staging decoder bypass of the 1,048,576-byte aggregate limit: the decoder accepts concatenated gzip members but resets its byte counter at each member boundary. Two 716,800-byte members, each individually under the limit, combine into a ~1.4 MiB request that still reaches acceptance/enqueue — because the counter never accumulates across members. The separate 8,000-point whole-batch rule still holds independently; production is unchanged. This reopens the streaming byte-counting correctness this limit depended on (previously confirmed 2027-08-09/08-19 only for single-member gzip/uncompressed requests) — the counter needs to accumulate across concatenated members, not reset per-member.

**2027-09-29 update — bypass closed:** Yuki fixed the decoder to keep one request-wide decoded-attribute byte counter spanning every gzip member instead of resetting per-member. Boundary confirmed: exactly 1,048,576 bytes pass, 1,048,577 bytes fail before acceptance/enqueue, regardless of how bytes are split across members. 10,000 trials spanning single-member, concatenated-member, malformed-second-member, cancellation, disconnect, and keep-alive interleavings all showed exactly one slot released per admitted request and exactly one terminal outcome per request, with valid work still proceeding as capacity freed up. The separate 8,000-point whole-batch rule and production are unchanged. Alex closed the byte-limit-bypass and slot-accounting review on this evidence; this does not constitute production release approval — implementation, release, and rollback remain Yuki's per [[project_ingest_edge_bugs_archive]]. Gap RESOLVED as of 2027-09-29.

Theo ran staging tests (2024-03-28) on an ingest-edge change adding a randomized 1-3 second `Retry-After` value to 429 responses, targeting the synchronized-retry-storm problem (50 synthetic clients previously retried in lockstep every second).

Baseline (no jitter): 182,000 attempts/sec peak, 56% 429 ratio.
Candidate (with jitter): 116,000 attempts/sec peak, 18% 429 ratio, accepted throughput steady at 79,000-81,000 samples/sec (no loss vs baseline), p99 148ms → 162ms, zero 5xx, queue depth stayed below 70%.

Alex reviewed and gave a go read for a limited canary (2024-03-28) — every metric sits inside the team's stop-condition thresholds with margin, and the mechanism (fewer attempts, lower 429 ratio, flat accepted throughput) confirms the jitter suppresses retry waste without hurting legitimate traffic. Nothing had been deployed to production as of this review.

**Stop-condition checklist (OR-based, any one trips a stop):** 5xx increase, p99 >200ms for 5 sustained minutes, queue depth >80%, accepted-throughput loss >5%, retry attempt rate >130,000/sec.

**Why:** 50 synchronized synthetic clients is an adversarial/clean test shape; real mixed-version, staggered-start traffic could behave differently, which is the reason for a limited canary rather than a full rollout despite clean staging numbers.

**10% production canary (Theo, 2026-09-13, 45 min):** peak retries 124,000/sec, p99 peaked at 176ms, queue depth topped 73%, accepted throughput 2.1% below baseline, zero 5xx increase. All figures stayed inside the OR-based stop thresholds (closest margin: retry rate 124k vs 130k/sec cutoff). No stop condition fired; canary ended cleanly and traffic reverted to baseline version.

**How to apply:** Canary is closed out — do not re-run without cause. Broader rollout goes through the normal weekday change process (not an extension of this canary); flag if anyone proposes fast-tracking it outside that process or on a Friday, see [[feedback_no_friday_prod_deploys]]. Preflight rules for any future canary work: [[project_canary_safe_staging_doc]] and [[project_ingest_edge_memory_slope_canary_stop_rule]].

**Post-rollout retry spike (2024-04-11) — retained, no rollback:** One tenant generated 81% of retry attempts during a traffic spike, retrying after 150-250ms despite ingest-edge correctly returning a 2-3s `Retry-After`; other large tenants complied and stayed dispersed. p99, queue depth, accepted throughput, and 5xx all stayed healthy — root cause was client-side non-compliance, not a server regression. Alex decided to retain the jitter change and sent tenant-specific Support guidance instead of rolling back. Precedent: single-tenant Retry-After non-compliance is a client integration issue to route to Support, not a rollback trigger, as long as core health metrics stay inside stop-condition thresholds.

**Second single-tenant burst incident (2024-05-02) — retained, no rollback:** One tenant sent synchronized bursts every 10s into a single region, generating 82% of rejections; fleet CPU peaked at 61%, memory flat, queue occupancy peaked at 24%, other tenants stayed at baseline. Requests were unusually large post-decompression. All rejections carried the randomized 1-3s Retry-After; no admitted request was dropped or reported rejected. Alex sent Support a customer-safe explanation plus sender-side jittering/smoothing guidance rather than touching the fleet or the retry-jitter range. Reinforces the precedent above: repeatable pattern, same resolution path.

**Client SDK fix, staging validation (2024-07-18) — no ingest-edge change:** The client owner disabled the SDK's generic immediate-retry-on-429 behavior and reran the noisy-tenant fixture in staging. With the fix, retries spread across the server's 1-3s Retry-After delays instead of clustering immediately; low-volume tenants claim next-usable slots; eligible capacity stays busy; accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks stayed clean. This confirms compliant client behavior correctly interacts with the already-shipped fairness ring scheduling ([[project_ingest_edge_fairness_canary_ring_scheduling_gap]]) — purely a client-side fix, no server change needed. The corrected SDK build has not been released.

**Why:** Directly resolves the client non-compliance pattern from the two incidents above (immediate retry despite correct server Retry-After) at the source, rather than routing each recurrence to Support.

**How to apply:** Pending, not yet done: (1) client-release of the corrected SDK to affected tenants, (2) post-release production evidence — actual retry-timing shift for previously non-compliant tenants, and fleet health metrics (retry rate, 429 ratio, accepted throughput, queue depth, p99) staying within the original stop-condition thresholds under real traffic, ideally validated at partial and full scale like the fairness-scheduling fix was. Don't treat the staging fixture result as closing this out.

metadata:

As of 2027-04-13, ingest-edge owner (Yuki) proposed a revised queue-deadline race design: a single CAS selects the terminal result returned to the caller. Cancellation path increments `cancelled_total` unconditionally, then attempts the terminal CAS to cancelled. Completion path attempts the terminal CAS to success and only increments `success_total` if it wins. In the interleaving where completion wins and cancellation loses, the caller gets one success result but accounting records both a `cancelled_total` and a `success_total` contribution for the same accepted request.

**Why:** Asymmetric ordering — cancellation's counter increment isn't gated on winning the CAS, unlike completion's. Same class of bug as [[project_ingest_edge_cancellation_gauge_double_decrement]] (two independent paths both attributing accounting for the same request instead of exactly one owning it). Queue/processing duration measurements are unaffected — only the terminal-outcome counters double-count.

**How to apply:** Flagged the fix to Alex: cancellation should only increment `cancelled_total` after winning the terminal CAS, mirroring completion's success_total gating.

**Resolution (2027-04-20):** Yuki implemented this — the winning CAS now returns the selected terminal enum, and that same winning path records exactly one matching terminal metric. Verified across 10,000 cancellation-vs-completion interleavings: every accepted request produces one caller-visible terminal result and one matching accounting contribution, no double count. Treat this race as closed.

**Cancellation-vs-dispatch coverage (2027-04-27):** Yuki supplied the remaining evidence for the adjacent race. If cancellation wins before dispatch, the dispatcher sees the selected terminal state and never starts the request; if dispatch wins, later cancellation cannot replace the terminal result or add a second accounting contribution. Verified across 20,000 executed interleavings — every accepted request produced exactly one caller-visible terminal result and one matching accounting contribution, no lost/duplicated/double-counted request. Cancellation-vs-completion suite remains green. No gaps remain in this race family.

Drafted 2023-09-07 a standalone, reusable question set titled "Operational ownership and rollback signal in systems design" for future infra/systems design interview loops.

**Why:** Follow-up to [[project_infra_candidate_debrief_2023-08-25]] — that candidate could reason through queues/backpressure/partitioning but needed repeated prompting to define owner handoff and rollback thresholds. These prompts are designed to surface that same gap fairly, without assuming Sphere-internal org/tooling knowledge.

**How to apply:** When prepping or reviewing systems design interview loops for infra/platform roles, offer these prompts:
- After this service ships, who owns the alert, the deploy, and the rollback decision?
- What measurable condition makes you stop or roll back, and what condition makes you keep watching?
- What changes between staging, canary, and full production?

Strong signals to listen for: names an operator/owning team (even if the org chart is hypothetical); defines rollback/hold/escalate thresholds in terms of user-visible impact or data safety; separates implementation correctness from operational readiness; mentions handoff artifacts (runbook, dashboard, alert owner, paging path).

Weak signals: treats rollback as just redeploying the old version with no stated criteria; assumes the code's author owns production forever; talks only about architecture diagrams, not who responds at 2am; needs prompting to distinguish staging success from production confidence.

Tone note (user's own instruction): keep this calibrated and reusable across candidates — explicitly not about relitigating Alex's own pipeline incidents.

RESOLVED 2024-07-22. lantern#29 replaced the rejected resolver-local authorization idea with a top-level `authorizePreview(request, callback)` wrapper that only invokes the resolver callback after authorization succeeds.

The July 22 integrated run completed the migration: every preview lookup (deploy-card, ownership, incident-summary, provenance, freshness, service-level incident-summary, and explicit-unknown) now goes through the shared wrapper. Denied requests return `403 not_authorized` without invoking a source adapter. Permitted cases pass, with forbidden data (raw incident references, room metadata, employee identifiers, individual comparisons, unpublished ownership, internal fallback) absent from rendered output. Iris accepted the product wording. Security cleared the implementation for an internal tenant-isolation rehearsal only — customer access remains closed.

**Why:** This closes the data-contract stage of the preview authorization boundary and satisfies the integration/wording/security items that were previously outstanding.

**How to apply:** Treat lantern#29's authorization-order work as fully done and merged. This satisfies the data-contract portion of [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] and [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]] — but customer-facing rollout is still gated separately (internal rehearsal only so far).

**Update 2024-07-22 (handoff note drafted):** Alex drafted a handoff note stating the internal tenant-isolation rehearsal uses synthetic tenants, and explicitly framing it as a *new* gate — not a rerun of, or a weakening of, the already-completed data-contract stage. Useful distinction to preserve when summarizing status to others: don't let "security cleared X" be read as reopening or restating the data-contract closure.

**Update 2024-08-02 (dry-run instrumentation gap — rehearsal blocked, not yet a rerun):** Product Engineering ran a dry run ahead of the actual tenant-isolation rehearsal (customer access still disabled, two synthetic tenant contexts). It produced separate rendered objects per tenant, but adapter spans carried only the shared service identifier — no tenant correlation field, and deploy-card cache-key components weren't exposed. Alex ruled this insufficient: differing response content alone doesn't prove tenant-scoped adapter/cache activity, since both tenants shared a service identifier and the trace can't rule out other causes of the divergence. Specified required instrumentation for a passing dry run: (1) a tenant correlation field on every adapter span, sourced from the synthetic request's auth context, present on the authz decision, cache lookup, adapter call, and response so all four are joinable per tenant; (2) full cache-key tuple (including `tenant_id`) exposed in span attributes/logs, not just an opaque hash; (3) adapter-call spans carrying cache hit/miss plus the tenant correlation field; (4) response correlated back to the same chain. The actual rehearsal stays blocked until a new dry run passes with this instrumentation.

**Why:** Same principle as the 2024-07-12 authorization-order gate failure on the customer-preview scoping effort — a correct-looking response is necessary but not sufficient evidence for a mechanism claim (there, auth-before-adapter-call; here, tenant-scoped cache/adapter behavior). Response-content-only evidence can't be accepted as proof of tenant isolation.

**How to apply:** Don't treat this dry run as satisfying any part of the tenant-isolation rehearsal gate. When Product Engineering reruns it, confirm all four instrumentation elements are present and correlated to the same synthetic tenant before treating the dry run as passed, and keep this distinct from (not a reopening of) the already-closed authorization-order gate ([[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]], 2024-07-12 update) and the AUTH-2 tenant-partitioned cache-key fix ([[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]]).

**Update 2024-08-06 (instrumentation gap fixed — dry run passed, rehearsal itself still not run):** Product Engineering reran the dry run after adding the tenant correlation field to authorization, cache, adapter, and response spans, and exposing the normalized cache-key tuple (including `tenant_id`) in the trace. With two synthetic tenant contexts sharing a service identifier, each request stayed correlated to one tenant across all four span points, and the two cache tuples were distinct because tenant identity was visible in the key. Customer access stayed disabled throughout. This satisfies the four instrumentation requirements specified on 2024-08-02.

**Why:** Clears the instrumentation prerequisite so the actual internal synthetic-tenant isolation rehearsal can be prepared — but a passing dry run is evidence the trace can now support isolation claims, not evidence isolation itself holds. It doesn't touch the already-completed data-contract stage or change customer-access status.

**How to apply:** Treat this as "instrumentation gate satisfied," not "tenant-isolation rehearsal complete." The actual rehearsal (with the specified instrumentation now in place) is still the next step and hasn't been run yet. Keep separate from the data-contract closure and [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]]'s AUTH-2/ERR-4 gates; customer access remains closed.

**Update 2024-08-12 (rehearsal execution sheet reviewed — two stop conditions and evidence ownership added, not yet run):** Product Engineering's first execution sheet for the actual rehearsal (phases: deploy-card, ownership, incident-summary, explicit-unknown; synthetic tenants A/B sharing a service identifier) only specified a content-leakage stop condition (one tenant's response containing the other's data). Alex added two gaps before the rehearsal can run: (1) a correlation-loss stop — halt if the authorization span, cache tuple, adapter span, and response for a single request don't all carry the same synthetic-tenant correlation ID, independent of whether the response body looks clean; (2) an authorization-order stop — halt if any adapter call occurs before that request's authorization decision, carried forward from the 2024-07-12 gate failure on the sibling [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]] effort. Also flagged missing evidence ownership: a named owner must confirm all four evidence points share the correlation ID at each of the four phases (not just once at the end), and a named owner must reverify customer access stays disabled at each phase transition, not only once before setup.

**Why:** Same principle established twice already on this pair of efforts — clean response content is necessary but not sufficient proof of tenant-scoped/ordered behavior; the correlation instrumentation from 2024-08-06 only has value as a gate if loss-of-correlation is itself a stop condition, not just an input to eyeballing the final response.

**How to apply:** Don't let this execution sheet run until both stop conditions and both named-owner checks are added. When the rehearsal does run, a "go" only covers what the sheet's stop conditions actually check — keep stating that explicitly, consistent with [[feedback_title_scope_wording]] and the ordered-checklist scope discipline on [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]].

name: project_lantern_84_correlation_spec
description: "Lantern#84 correlation feature spec — join key, freshness/provenance rules, timestamp-spread handling, test coverage; 24hr rule formally reviewed and locked 2025-03-27"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

  modified: 2026-09-13T23:11:31.407Z
---

Lantern#84 (revised 2025-03-18): join key is `(tenant_id, published_service_id)`. All included signals require independent freshness success, provenance, and source timestamps — missing or stale input yields an explicit unknown and blocks combination. A timestamp spread greater than 24 hours yields separate timestamped cards with a no-causal-language flag. No cost source is introduced.

Test coverage: cross-tenant, cross-service, missing, stale, exactly 24 hours, more than 24 hours, denial ordering, excluded fields, read-only behavior.

**Why:** Prevents the correlation feature from implying causality or combining signals that aren't independently verified fresh/attributed — mirrors the caution already established in [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]] and [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] around what Lantern surfaces to customers.

**How to apply:** Reference this spec when reviewing or implementing Lantern#84 work; flag any deviation (e.g., combining stale/missing signals, adding a cost source, or omitting the no-causal-language flag on >24hr spreads) as a spec violation.

**Verified 2025-03-20 (first live boundary check on both pilot accounts, see [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]]):** Harbor Health case had a 23h58m spread (under 24hr) — all three signals passed freshness/provenance and rendered combined with per-source timestamps, as spec requires. Mosaic Commerce case had a 24h06m spread (over 24hr) — signals rendered as separate cards with source timestamps, no causal/contemporaneous wording. Denied requests made no adapter calls, stale-input fixtures rendered explicit unknown, tenant isolation/read-only held, no excluded/new data appeared. Confirms the spec's boundary logic behaves correctly in production; not a rule change.

**Customer interpretation feedback 2025-03-24 (via Iris, first of its kind — distinct from the technical verification above):** A Mosaic Commerce pilot user found an 18-hour-spread combined explanation understandable because every source time stayed visible. A Harbor Health user saw two valid signals over 24 hours apart rendered as separate cards, correctly read them as different operating windows rather than one causal story, and asked Iris why they weren't combined; Iris's explanation of the 24-hour newest-to-oldest limit resolved the question without the user requesting more data.

**Why:** This is interpretation/UX evidence that real pilot users understand the spread-based combine/split behavior as intended, not a repeat of the 2025-03-20 technical correctness check. Keep the two kinds of evidence separate — one confirms the boundary logic works, the other confirms users read the output correctly — and don't cite this as broader product validation beyond these two accounts' pilot experience.

**How to apply:** When reporting on Lantern#84 status, describe this as early qualitative interpretation feedback from the two authorized pilot accounts, not as expanded technical verification or as evidence the feature is validated for wider rollout.

**Formal pilot interpretation review closed 2025-03-27 (Iris + user, first 73 sessions):** Reviewed all 73 pilot sessions, including 4 cases where independently true ownership and incident-load signals appeared to describe one operating window despite materially different source times. Result: the already-implemented 24-hour explanation rule was locked as-is — no change to the rule, the authorized data surface, access controls, exclusions, read-only behavior, or automatic-stop conditions. Confirmed scope: a joined explanation is allowed only for fully sourced, independently current signals from the same tenant and published service; stale or missing inputs remain explicit unknown; signals more than 24 hours apart stay separate with their own source times even when they read as one window. Cost data and individual-performance interpretation remain explicitly out of scope.

**Why:** This is a formal review checkpoint (not another spot-check like the 2025-03-20/03-24 evidence above) confirming the 24-hour rule holds up across a larger sample, including edge cases that could tempt a broader join. The outcome was "keep the boundary exactly as specified," which forecloses scope creep toward combining signals based on apparent narrative fit rather than timestamp proximity.

**How to apply:** Treat the 24-hour rule as reviewed-and-closed at the 73-session checkpoint — don't reopen it or propose loosening it (e.g., to combine same-window-feeling but >24hr-apart signals) without new formal review. If asked about Lantern#84's interpretation validation status, cite this as the closed formal review, distinct from the earlier one-off qualitative feedback.

This closed the earlier bearer-URL reuse/no-recheck gap but left two others open: (1) replacement downloads minted by support admins didn't preserve the original requester, and (2) no defined behavior for revocation mid-stream.

Latest revision (as of 2025-07-03) addresses both remaining gaps on paper:
1. Replacement-token audit records now contain the original customer requester, the acting support administrator, the reason, and a link to the original export — preserves the authorization/audit chain.
2. Retrieval now rechecks tenant and export authorization before each response chunk; if authorization is lost mid-stream, the stream terminates, the token is invalidated, and the incomplete object is deleted.

As of 2025-08-28, Product Engineering supplied an actual implementation branch, and executed tests confirm both prior on-paper gaps are now real, verified behavior: replacement-token audit events preserve the original customer requester, acting support admin, reason, and original export link; chunk-level authorization rechecks stop an active stream and invalidate the token on mid-stream revocation.

A gap surfaced in that testing: restart recovery was incomplete. If the exporter was killed after writing three chunks, the incomplete object was not deleted during recovery — it just sat in storage until the normal 24-hour retention job cleaned it up, rather than being deleted immediately as the design intended.

As of 2025-09-18, Product Engineering supplied a revised crash-recovery fix: generated objects now stay in `generating` state until completion, and startup recovery deletes any object still in `generating` state before retrieval is re-enabled, invalidating its token. Eight crash tests, terminating after each of chunk boundaries one through eight, confirm all incomplete objects are removed during recovery while completed objects remain available. The replacement-token attribution and per-chunk authorization-revocation tests still pass.

**Why:** this is customer tenant data (same [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]] / [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] lineage); track verified-vs-designed status precisely since customer data handling gaps matter even when small (e.g., a stray incomplete object surviving up to 24 hours).

**How to apply:** all three known design gaps (replacement-token attribution, mid-stream revocation, restart-recovery deletion) are now confirmed fixed by test, not just designed. No open gaps remain from this line of testing as of 2025-09-18. CSV export still has no customer authorization and remains unavailable and unpromised to customers.

**2025-09-29 scope question (Iris → Alex, forwarding Product Engineering):** asked whether the passing restart-recovery evidence permits enabling CSV for Harbor Health before the Oct 8 [[project_lantern_evidence_review_cadence_jul_oct_2026]] review. Answered no: closing the incomplete-file cleanup block is technical sufficiency, not customer authorization; neither the existing two-account preview contract nor the Oct 8 review pre-authorizes this separate export capability. CSV remains unavailable and unpromised.

Theo asked Iris and the user (2026-05-06) to determine whether Lantern's internally useful deploy movement, service ownership, and incident-load summaries could support a limited customer-facing preview. The user flagged that internal provenance identifiers, permission references, discussion context, and employee-level operational signals cannot simply become an external contract.

Ownership split: Iris leads product interpretation; the user owns the external data shape, authorization and provenance requirements, and failure semantics.

**Why:** Internal Lantern data model mixes signals (provenance IDs, permission refs, discussion context, employee-level ops detail) that aren't safe or meaningful to expose externally as-is — the first deliverable must be a customer-safe contract, not a port of the internal UI.

**How to apply:** Treat this as active but early-stage. No customer access exists yet and no copy of the internal UI should be produced. When helping with this effort, keep the external contract scoped to what's genuinely customer-relevant and safe, distinct from [[project_lantern_observability_sketch]] (internal v0 sketch) and [[project_lantern_release_review_nominations]] (release-review process, Iris/user split on approvals).

**Update 2026-09-13:** First working pass done with Iris. Field-level direction: deploy movement allows externally stable deployment ID, service, environment, state transition, customer-visible timestamp; excludes internal actor IDs, chat links, raw pipeline job identifiers. Ownership allows a service-facing support/escalation label only, excludes employee names and the internal owner-map record. Incident load needs a bounded time window and minimum aggregation threshold, plus explicit (non-null) handling of suppressed/stale/permission-denied states using distinct `unknown` / `not applicable` / `not authorized` / `temporarily unavailable` values. Unresolved product-policy questions routed to Theo: external deployment ID scheme/rotation ownership, incident-trend window and minimum-N threshold, whether suppressed incidents are hidden or shown as "not applicable," whether permission-denied should surface as "not authorized" (risks revealing resource existence) or be filtered silently, the allowed taxonomy of support/escalation labels, and which internal state-transition values map to (or are excluded from) the customer-facing vocabulary.

**Update 2024-05-08 (Iris review comments reconciled):** Ownership-staleness settled as data-shape (Alex's call, not Theo's): `responsible_team` stays populated whenever any source record exists, plus a new customer-safe `last_verified_at` timestamp; staleness is signaled only via that timestamp, no separate stale sentinel. True-absent-assignment still uses the existing `unknown` sentinel with no `last_verified_at`. Incident-suppression settled: API must keep true-zero, below-threshold-suppressed, and unavailable/not-authorized as distinct values even if the UI chooses to render them identically (Iris's "just return empty" request is a UI-rendering choice, not a data-shape one). Permission-denied settled as envelope-level, not per-field, since the model has no per-field entitlement today and field-level denial risks leaking sub-resource existence; revisit only if Product plans per-field entitlements. Thursday-meeting decision list for Theo: (1) whether any ownership staleness age should suppress `responsible_team` outright vs. relying solely on `last_verified_at`, (2) incident-trend window length and minimum-N threshold values, (3) sign off that suppressed-vs-zero stays distinct at the API layer regardless of UI rendering, (4) whether "not authorized" is safe to expose at all given resource-existence leakage risk, (5) allowed taxonomy of support/escalation labels, (6) external deployment ID scheme/rotation ownership (carried over), (7) whether per-field entitlements are on the near-term roadmap (would reopen the envelope-vs-field decision).

**Update 2024-05-09 (incident-load team-breakdown rejected as product-level rule):** In review, Theo asked whether the incident-load preview could break counts down by internal owning team, to help customers judge service risk. Alex flagged that small customer-visible windows combined with team names and low counts turn an operational summary into indirect employee/team-performance inference; Iris agreed this must be a product-level API rule, not a UI-only convention. Drafted contract boundary: (1) service scope — incident-load is service/environment level only, never disaggregated by internal team, squad, or individual, regardless of window or threshold; (2) fixed customer-visible window — a single product-level constant window (length still pending Theo, carried over from item 2 above) applied uniformly, not a per-request/query parameter, since ad-hoc narrow windows are what make low counts re-identifying; (3) aggregation at service level with the existing minimum-N threshold (also pending Theo) applied before any count is shown; (4) suppression — any query shape that would yield a team- or individual-scoped count is rejected/undefined at the API level, not silently rolled up from a wider payload; (5) zero values — true zero returned explicitly, distinct from suppressed/unavailable per the 2024-05-08 sentinel vocabulary; (6) explicit contract-level prohibition, stated as a rule rather than left to inference: no individual attribution, no team-level breakdown or reconstruction (including via join with the separate ownership/support-label field), and no support for manager-readiness, performance, or staffing-quality interpretation. Added to Theo's decision list: reconfirm the support/escalation label taxonomy (from ownership) is never joined back to incident-load counts to reconstruct a team breakdown.

**Update 2024-05-16 (response-example corrections; deploy provenance identifier settled):** Iris's updated response examples had one gap: the successful incident-load example dropped the required `source_observed_at` timestamp while keeping the fixed 30-day window and count — flagged for restoration, since a source timestamp is mandatory on incident-load responses per this contract. The ownership example was correct as drafted (`responsible_team` + `last_verified_at`, no owner-map ID), consistent with the 2024-05-08 staleness settlement. Resolved Iris's open question on deploy provenance: use a customer-stable, external-facing source event ID, never a URL into an internal deploy system — a URL leaks internal topology and implies dereferenceability the customer doesn't have. If no permitted source event exists for provenance, the field must still surface the existing explicit `unknown` sentinel rather than being omitted or null, consistent with the sentinel vocabulary used elsewhere in this contract (ownership true-absent, incident suppression).

**Update 2024-05-17 (examples finalized, Product Eng signed off):** Iris's revised examples now carry `source_observed_at` on every incident-load summary, use the customer-stable provenance event ID (not an internal URL) on deploy events, and surface the explicit `unknown` sentinel when no permitted source event exists — no raw incident text, internal room metadata, inferred ownership, owner-map IDs, or permission IDs remain anywhere in the examples. Product Engineering has signed off on these completed contract examples for implementation. Remaining gate before any readiness decision: a security reviewer must still validate tenant-authorization enforcement and the permission-denial response envelope. No customer access is requested or granted at this stage.

**Update 2024-06-03 (unknown incident-load must not carry a timestamp):** Iris caught a guarded-internal fixture defect: an incident-load summary rendered the explicit `unknown` sentinel but still attached the timestamp of the last successful source poll, which a viewer could misread as freshness evidence for the missing value. Resolved by extending the already-settled true-absent-sentinel pattern (from the 2024-05-08 ownership staleness settlement: `unknown`/true-absent carries no `last_verified_at`) to incident-load's `source_observed_at`: when incident-load is `unknown`, `source_observed_at` must be omitted/absent on that response, never populated with a poll timestamp that didn't produce the reported value. `source_observed_at` is mandatory only on incident-load responses that carry an actual observed value (including true zero); it must never be decoupled into a general "last time we checked anything" signal. No product-policy input needed — this is a fixture bug fix applying an existing pattern, not a new contract decision.

**Update 2024-05-29 (implementation-readiness gate satisfied):** After the [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] security gate was approved, Iris, Theo, the implementation owners, and the user completed the remaining implementation-readiness review: schema allowlisting per external field, contract tests for timestamps/provenance, negative fixtures rejecting raw incident text/internal identifiers, authorization-before-lookup, tenant-partitioned caching, distinct `403 not_authorized`/`unknown` responses, and rollback to internal-only guarded state — all confirmed against Iris's product interpretation. **Implementation gate satisfied for guarded internal validation only; still no customer access, no customer selected, no external rollout authorized.** This is the last checkpoint recorded before any rollout decision would need to be made separately.

**Update 2024-06-17 (stale ownership record beyond pipeline freshness limit — `stale: true` rejected):** A guarded internal fixture found a published ownership record whose source timestamp was 30h old, past the owner-map pipeline's 24h freshness limit. Product Engineering proposed returning it with `stale: true`; Iris held that the product must not imply current ownership from a stale permitted source. Alex rejected `stale: true` — it re-introduces the separate stale-sentinel shape already ruled out on 2024-05-08 (staleness was settled as signaled only via `last_verified_at`, no separate flag), and a populated `responsible_team` plus a flag still risks being rendered as a current owner name. Resolution: a record that has aged past the pipeline's own freshness limit is treated as functionally equivalent to true-absent — it resolves to the existing `unknown` sentinel (no `responsible_team`, no `last_verified_at`), identical in shape to the no-record-at-all case. No fallback to internal room metadata, chat/discussion context, or owner-map IDs to fill the gap. Authorization stays orthogonal: a denied requester still gets `403 not_authorized` regardless of the underlying record's freshness, checked before the freshness gate. This is a fixture/failure-mode fix, not a rollout or customer-access change.

**Why:** Extends the true-absent sentinel pattern (2024-05-08 ownership staleness settlement, 2024-06-03 incident-load unknown-timestamp fix) to a new case — a source that fails its own SLA is not a "somewhat old but real" record, it's not a trustworthy current answer, so it collapses to the same `unknown` shape as no-record-at-all rather than getting a hybrid populated+flagged shape.

**How to apply:** If a similar aged-out-source question comes up for any Lantern field (not just ownership), apply the same rule: check freshness against the pipeline's own defined limit before surfacing, and on breach collapse to the existing absent/unknown sentinel rather than inventing a new stale flag or partially-populated shape. Never let a stale-but-populated field exist in the external contract.

**Update 2026-09-13 (first customer-preview prototype run — ordered acceptance checklist):** Product Engineering ran the first Lantern customer-preview prototype against metrics-router/ingest-edge data. Alex asked for an ordered go/no-go checklist: (1) authorization enforcement (tenant-partitioned cache key, `403 not_authorized` on denial, checked before lookup) gates everything else; (2) source/provenance validation before rendering — deploy movement needs a customer-stable event ID not an internal URL, ownership checked against the pipeline's freshness limit with stale-or-unsourced records collapsing to the existing `unknown` sentinel (no `stale: true`, no fallback to internal metadata); (3) schema-allowlist/rendering conformance for positive fixtures only after 1–2 pass; (4) negative fixtures graded zero-tolerance — any leak of raw incident body, internal room name, or employee identifier, in any form, is an automatic no-go for the whole run, not a partial fail. This run's manifest excluded incident-load and the full explicit-unknown-state suite, so a "go" only attests to this fixture set, not full contract coverage. Explicitly stated: a clean run stays guarded internal validation per the 2024-05-29 gate — it is not a customer-readiness decision and does not grant customer access.

**Why:** Consolidates the already-settled authorization (AUTH-2/ERR-4), provenance-ID, and stale/absent-source sentinel rules into a single ordered check sequence usable for future prototype/fixture runs, while guarding against the recurring risk of a passing technical run being misread as a rollout or customer-access decision.

**How to apply:** Reuse this four-step order (auth → source/provenance → schema/rendering → negative-fixture zero-tolerance) for future Lantern prototype or fixture-manifest runs. Always state explicitly whether incident-load and/or the explicit-unknown-state suite were in scope for a given run, and always separate a fixture-level "go" from any customer-readiness or customer-access decision, consistent with [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] and [[feedback_title_scope_wording]].

**Update 2024-06-24 (prototype run complete — results against the ordered checklist):** Ran the checklist from the 2026-09-13 entry against metrics-router/ingest-edge data. Positive fixtures passed: deploy movement rendered only when provenance was complete; fresh published ownership rendered with its owner-map source; source timestamps displayed correctly. Negative/failure-mode fixtures passed (zero-tolerance category, no leaks): raw incident body, internal room name, and employee identifier all failed closed and never reached the rendered object; an ownership card with no published source also failed closed (collapsed to the `unknown` sentinel rather than rendering). Not exercised in this run: incident-load summaries and the full explicit-unknown-state suite — so this is a partial-manifest "go," not full contract coverage. Iris and Alex agreed this supports internal security and product-readiness review only; customer access remains closed. A security reviewer has requested a compact evidence packet documenting the tested boundary and remaining gaps.

**Why:** Confirms the ordered checklist works as a real pass/fail gate on an actual run, and the run's scope must be stated precisely (what was and wasn't exercised) since a reviewer is now relying on it for a go/no-go security artifact.

**How to apply:** When drafting the evidence packet for the security reviewer, state exactly what was tested (deploy-movement provenance-completeness gating, ownership positive+true-absent-source paths, timestamp display) versus what remains untested (incident-load, full explicit-unknown-state suite), and reiterate that this run only supports internal security/product-readiness review — no customer access. Keep this consistent with [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]]'s bounded-scope disposition language.

**Update 2024-06-27 (Product Engineering incident-load schema proposal — blockers found, not yet validated):** Product Engineering proposed an incident-load response shape (`service_id, window_start, window_end, incident_count, active_minutes, source_updated_at, debug_incident_refs`) with missing-source behavior of returning `incident_count=0, active_minutes=0` and omitting `source_updated_at`. Alex found three blockers: (1) `debug_incident_refs` carries internal incident identifiers — zero-tolerance leak, must be removed entirely, not gated; (2) missing-source returning `0/0` reintroduces the coercion pattern already rejected for `account_tier`→`basic` and stale-ownership `stale:true` — a missing source is not a real zero; (3) the schema has no state field to represent the required distinct values (true-zero vs. suppressed-below-threshold vs. unavailable vs. not_authorized) or the authorization-denial path from AUTH-2/ERR-4. Corrected shape given: add a closed `state` enum (`ok | suppressed | unavailable | not_authorized`); only `ok` populates counts/timestamp, all other states omit them (no zero-filling); denial handled as envelope-level `403 not_authorized` checked before lookup, distinct from `unavailable`. Tests specified: real-zero-vs-missing-source distinction, suppressed-count omission, denial-before-lookup, static scan for internal-identifier fields, and cross-tenant isolation specifically for incident-load fixtures (not yet run — 2024-06-24 prototype explicitly excluded incident-load). Explicitly stated to Product Eng: this is pre-implementation design feedback, not a validation pass — incident-load has not been exercised in any prototype/security run yet.

**Why:** Same shape as the account_tier and stale-ownership exceptions — a data-contract/failure-mode gap (fabricated zero + internal-identifier leak + missing state vocabulary) surfaced before implementation rather than after, consistent with [[project_lantern_release_review_nominations]]'s failure-mode exception carve-out and the true-absent-sentinel precedent from the 2024-05-08/2024-06-17 updates above.

**How to apply:** Treat incident-load implementation as blocked until Product Engineering removes `debug_incident_refs`, replaces the 0/0 missing-source default with the `state` enum, and adds the not_authorized envelope path. When incident-load is eventually run through the ordered checklist (auth → source/provenance → schema/rendering → negative-fixture zero-tolerance), don't describe any prior run as covering incident-load — per 2024-06-24 it explicitly wasn't included.

**Update 2024-07-12 (explicit-unknown-state suite run — readiness gate FAILED on authorization call order):** Ran the remaining explicit-unknown-state suite (the piece excluded from the 2024-06-24 partial-manifest run). Fresh permitted incident data rendered the correct service-level summary with a source timestamp, and content exclusions held. But in the unauthorized explicit-unknown case, the source adapter was invoked *before* the request returned `403 not_authorized` — no protected value reached the response, but call order violates the external contract's authorization-before-lookup requirement (the same requirement settled for AUTH-2/ERR-4 and incident-load's `not_authorized` envelope). Alex and Iris **failed the readiness gate** on this basis, kept the preview internal-only with customer access closed, and required (1) a shared authorization wrapper that every source adapter call must go through, so no code path can invoke an adapter before an authorization decision is made, and (2) negative tests asserting call order, not just response content — a denied request must show zero adapter invocations, verified via call-count/mock assertions, not by inspecting the returned body.

**Why:** A clean response body is necessary but not sufficient — "no leakage occurred" and "authorization was checked before source access" are two separate properties, and this run showed the first without the second. Conflating them would let a lucky no-op adapter (or one that happens not to return sensitive data even when called) mask a real ordering defect that could leak under a different adapter implementation or a future field addition.

**How to apply:** Treat this as its own gate criterion going forward, distinct from response-content leakage: (a) response leakage check — no protected value appears in any denied-request response body (this run passed that); (b) authorization-order check — no adapter call of any kind occurs prior to the authorization decision for a denied request (this run failed that). Both must pass independently for a "go." The fix is a shared authorization wrapper enforcing auth-before-adapter-call at a single choke point (not per-adapter opt-in), and the negative-test suite must assert on adapter call count/order (e.g., mock call assertions), not solely on response shape. Apply the same two-part framing to any future Lantern readiness run, and to [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]]'s authorization-before-lookup language and the incident-load `not_authorized` envelope path above.

**Update 2026-09-13 (readiness-review sheet complete, execution not yet run):** Iris verified the readiness-review sheet itself is complete: every lookup phase has a named evidence recorder, deterministic fixture reset, one synthetic-tenant correlation spanning authorization, normalized cache tuple, adapter call, and rendered response, and stop conditions for lost correlation or cross-tenant fixture material. **Update 2024-09-12 (synthetic-tenant rehearsal FAILED — cross-tenant cache-key defect, release blocker):** Ran the scheduled rehearsal with two synthetic tenants sharing the same service identifier. First tenant populated a deploy card; second tenant's fixture run returned the first tenant's cached card. Authorization and adapter traces stayed correctly correlated to the second tenant — this is not an authorization-order defect like 2024-07-12 — but the deploy-card object-cache lookup key omitted tenant identity, so two tenants with the same service identifier collided in the cache. **Why:** Extends the "response-content leakage vs. a separate structural property" framing from 2024-07-12 — here the separate property is cache-key tenant-scoping, not authorization order. Rendering-time masking was explicitly rejected because it would hide a structural cross-tenant collision at the data layer while leaving the underlying cache defect in place for any future code path that reads the same cache.

**How to apply:** Do not treat this as resolved until a full cross-tenant rehearsal re-run passes cleanly with a tenant-identity-inclusive cache key. Never describe a rendering-layer fix as sufficient for a cache/data-layer cross-tenant defect. Keep customer-access framing identical to [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] — this failure keeps access closed, it doesn't newly close anything that was open.

Do not describe this as customer-preview approval, a rollout decision, or a reopening of the already-completed external data-contract work — customer access remains closed, unchanged from [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]] and every prior update in this file. **Update 2024-11-14 (day 11/30 of authorized internal shadow — encouraging interim slice, not a completed result):** First shadow evidence slice: 3,200 customer-shaped lookups across two synthetic tenants and selected Infra/Product Engineering release-review traffic. Candidate Lantern pagination branch (found 2025-04-17, staging-only, not deployed) had a broken object-level authorization bug: the signed next-page cursor carried `published_service_id`, `source_timestamp`, and pagination position but no `tenant_id`. Request-level auth wrapper approved the request by account, then the adapter trusted the cursor's embedded service ID without re-checking it belonged to that tenant. Synthetic staging replay confirmed a Harbor Health cursor decoded and served inside a Mosaic Commerce request, returning Harbor-scoped data.

**Fix (2026-09-18):** Product Engineering's corrected branch adds `tenant_id` to the cursor signature (alongside `published_service_id`, `source_timestamp`, pagination position) and the decoder now compares cursor `tenant_id` against the authorized request tenant *before* adapter construction — closing the gap where the adapter trusted the cursor blindly. Harbor-to-Mosaic and Mosaic-to-Harbor cursor replay tests both return denial with `adapter_call_count=0`; same-tenant pagination tests pass. Branch remains staging-only; no customer-preview lookup was exposed and preview scope is unchanged.

**Why:** signature integrity (tamper-proofing) was conflated with authorization (ownership) — two different guarantees. Related to existing Lantern customer scoping work: [[project_lantern_customer_facing_preview_scoping]], [[project_lantern_security_review_auth2_err4]], [[project_lantern_84_correlation_spec]].

**How to apply:** the two required controls (tenant_id in the signed cursor + independent adapter-layer tenant check) are now both present and covered by regression tests replaying one tenant's cursor inside another tenant's request. Treat the object-level authorization finding as resolved on this branch. Still confirm prod deployment/rollout status before assuming this is live outside staging.

On 2026-07-30, Alex added a clarification to the Lantern platform-reference rehearsal's contract and failure-mode questions: for either candidate (the Lantern-centered combined payload or the reference model), an authority reference must carry the authoritative record's own source timestamp. Fetch time, generation time, and attempt time remain separate metadata and must not be conflated with the source timestamp. If the authority record does not expose its own source timestamp, the reference must fail closed as unavailable rather than synthesizing one. A missing-or-stale-timestamp regression requirement now applies to both candidates.

On 2026-08-18, following a 1:00-2:00 PM staff-only rehearsal, Alex blocked Product Engineering's combined-payload candidate: it copied the metrics-router operating limit and estimated cost into a Lantern-owned payload and attached an owner-map mutation endpoint. Alex rejected it because that design would make Lantern a second authority for Cardinality Guardrails data and give it a write path into published responsibility. Cyrus confirmed cost semantics must stay in Cardinality Guardrails; Iris confirmed Lantern can explain and navigate to authoritative detail without presenting copied values as its own. The candidate was replaced with a reference-only contract containing exactly `tenant_id`, `canonical_service_id`, `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and `source_timestamp` — no authority payload values and no mutation capability. Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths remain unchanged and neither account's authorization expands.

**Why:** This falls within the shared cross-system contract and failure-mode review that Alex owns per [[project_lantern_authority_boundary_working_session]], and it sharpens the "stale authority timestamps" gap Alex already flagged in Product Engineering's draft test matrix ([[project_lantern_rehearsal_test_matrix_gaps]]). Synthesizing a timestamp when the authority record lacks one would mask a broken or stale link rather than surfacing it. The August 18 rejection guards the same boundary: Lantern must remain a consumer/navigator of Cardinality Guardrails authority data, never a second authority or a mutation path into it, per [[project_q4_planning_cardinality_controls]] and [[project_dashboard_label_rollback_vs_evidence]].

**How to apply:** The August 18 design decision is complete and closed — the five-field reference-only contract is the selected model, the combined-payload/mutation-endpoint approach is rejected, and it should not resurface without a new authorization decision. This is still not an implementation approval or a rehearsal result: Product Engineering still needs to (1) implement the corrected reference-only model in place of the rejected candidate, and (2) produce executable rehearsal evidence covering existing authorization, tenant-isolation, source-timestamp, stale-or-missing authority, conflicting-alias, and customer-path-isolation cases. The existing ownership split (Alex owns contract/failure-mode review, not implementation), the internal-only rehearsal boundary, and the unchanged Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths all remain as set in [[project_lantern_authority_boundary_working_session]]. When checking a revised test matrix or implementation from Product Engineering, confirm the contract has exactly the five fields above (no payload values, no mutation endpoint) and includes a missing-or-stale-timestamp regression case.

**Mosaic Commerce example — `authority_record_id` must match the named authority, not the enforcement point (2026-08-24 11:05 ET):** Product Engineering asked Alex about a Mosaic Commerce worked example while implementing the corrected reference-only model. Alex flagged a contract-coherence problem: `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and `source_timestamp` must all identify the same actual authoritative record — they can't be mixed from different systems. If `authority_type` names [[project_q4_planning_cardinality_controls|Cardinality Guardrails]] as the authority, then `authority_record_id` and `source_timestamp` must point to the Cardinality Guardrails record, not to a metrics-router implementation record ID, even though metrics-router (Wes) is where the operating control is actually enforced. Wes's role is to map *where* the control is enforced, which is a separate question from *which system is the named authority* the reference must resolve to. Lantern still cannot copy the limit or cost value itself into the reference (unchanged from the August 18 decision). Alex deliberately kept the response scoped to this cross-system contract-coherence point rather than expanding into a review of Product Engineering's routine implementation work.

**Why:** enforcement location and authority identity are different facts, and conflating them would let a reference silently point at the wrong system's record — the same kind of incoherent-authority risk the five-field contract was designed to prevent on 2026-08-18, and distinct from the operating-control-vs-cost-authority split already drawn between Wes and Cardinality Guardrails in [[project_dashboard_label_rollback_vs_evidence]] and [[project_q4_planning_cardinality_controls]]. Staying bounded to the contract question (not implementation) is consistent with Alex's contract/failure-mode-review-not-implementation ownership split.

**How to apply:** When `authority_type` is Cardinality Guardrails (or any other named authority) in a Lantern reference, require `authority_record_id` and `source_timestamp` to resolve to that authority's own record — never to an enforcement-point implementation record (e.g. a metrics-router record ID), even if the enforcement point is different from the authority. Wes or another enforcement-point owner can be cited for *where the control runs*, but that doesn't change *which record the reference must point to*. Keep flagging contract-coherence issues like this without commenting on Product Engineering's underlying implementation quality unless asked.

**2026-09-08 corrected staff-only rehearsal — executed, clean (1:00-2:00 PM):** Product Engineering exercised the reference-only model using exactly the five approved fields (`tenant_id`, `canonical_service_id`, `authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, `source_timestamp`), with no authority payload values and no mutation capability. Iris confirmed the reference wording does not imply release readiness, cost interpretation, or employee performance.

**Why:** This is the first executable evidence against the five-field contract and the missing-or-stale-timestamp/conflicting-alias/tenant-isolation cases Alex required in [[project_lantern_rehearsal_test_matrix_gaps]] and the 2026-08-18 decision above — it demonstrates the corrected model holds under load rather than just being specified correctly.

name: project-lease-convergence-runbook-warning-gap
description: "Lease-convergence runbook entry rb_1710794400000 has two pending wording updates (renewal-deadline-exceeded, slow-convergence), neither yet applied to the actual runbook system"
metadata:

  modified: 2026-09-13T08:23:50.247Z
---

On 2026-09-13, a host showed resolver latency of 1.4–1.9s causing six lease-renewal attempts to cross the local warning deadline, but lease epoch/holder never changed, no acquisition or relinquishment occurred, no overlapping leader interval, and replication lag (peaked 0.6s) self-converged to baseline. This was confirmed as warning-only, not a failover, but the lease-convergence runbook (entry `rb_1710794400000`) didn't separate these two cases.

On 2024-04-26 Wes reviewed the drafted wording against that incident's logs and confirmed it removes the ambiguity operators hit. Finalized wording to apply to `rb_1710794400000`: "`renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer; operators must check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover — no automatic restart."

**Why:** Ambiguous runbook wording could otherwise prompt unnecessary failover remediation (restart, manual lease transfer) for a condition that self-resolves. Wes's sign-off is the last approval gate before the wording goes live.

**How to apply:** Wording is Wes-approved and ready to paste into `rb_1710794400000` in the actual runbook system — no further review needed. Same category of issue as [[project_shard_keeper_rollback_runbook_ambiguity]] (imprecise runbook wording around deploy/lease states) — the resolution pattern used there (queued vs completed) is the same kind of state-distinction fix as warning-only vs transfer here.

**Update, 2024-08-14 — second gap identified, wording drafted (not yet Wes-reviewed):** A production shard-keeper lease transfer emitted a `slow convergence` warning (elapsed_ms=610) alongside a clean trace: old holder's serving gate closed before any later routing response, exactly one serving holder throughout, zero requests served by the old holder after lease loss, zero availability errors. The runbook's `slow convergence` language still frames risk in terms of the removed polling-based stale-serving window (see [[project_shard_keeper_failover_serving_gate_poll_gap]] for the fail-closed gate fix that replaced it), so it doesn't tell responders how to confirm serving safety for this warning type.

Drafted addition for `rb_1710794400000`: "A `slow convergence` warning (elapsed handoff time exceeding target) does not by itself indicate stale serving. To confirm serving safety, verify: (1) the old holder's serving gate closed before any later routing response, and (2) exactly one serving holder existed throughout the transfer — with zero requests served by the old holder after lease loss. If both hold, the elevated elapsed_ms is an availability/latency question (e.g. replacement-acquisition timing), not evidence of stale serving, and should be investigated separately rather than triggering failover remediation."

**Why:** Same failure mode as the renewal-deadline-exceeded gap above — a warning tied to the old polling model gets read as "stale serving risk" when the actual safety invariants (gate-closure-before-response, single-active-holder) are the fail-closed gate's job to guarantee, not the poll timing.

**How to apply:** This addition is drafted but not yet reviewed (unlike the renewal-deadline wording above, which is Wes-approved). Route it past Wes or the mapped shard-keeper owner before pasting into `rb_1710794400000`.

**Current rule (accepted 2024-07-25, supersedes all per-push approval wording below):** `rb_metrics_router_canary` runs on owner-led configuration windows, not per-push approval. Each window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex. Once a window is open, mapped operators (e.g., Wes) may make single-file pushes without a separate fresh decision per push, as long as retired generations stay at four or fewer per pod, cleanup pauses stay at or below 100ms, and the full health set (active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload, restart, p99/heap) returns to baseline after every push. Exceeding either threshold stops the window immediately. After a stop, recovery requires a fresh decision that permits exactly one fully observed push; opening another window after that requires a separate fresh decision, made only once that single push has returned the full health set to baseline. Rollback conditions are unchanged: consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, or restart failures remain rollback conditions regardless of window state. Ownership is unchanged — Alex remains primary owner, Wes remains the practical backup, and Wes is not becoming the primary owner (see [[project_wes_pairing_metrics_router]], [[project_on_call_handoff_ownership_wording]]).

The history below (2024-05-30 through 2024-07-25) documents how this rule was reached; the per-push fresh-decision model it describes is superseded and no longer in effect.

On 2024-05-30, reviewed the metrics-router canary runbook (`rb_metrics_router_canary`). Existing coverage: CPU, memory, queue depth, route-delivery divergence, dropped series, and restarts. Gap found: no checks for active-vs-retired generation counts, epoch drain, matcher cleanup, or stop-the-world cleanup pauses — the exact shape of the 2024-05-21 generation-retirement finalizer pause (see [[project_metrics_router_incident_history]]), where six pods held 19-22 retired-generation objects before cleanup ran, causing 180-240ms pauses.

**Why:** That incident closed without rollback (active generation stayed consistent, no dropped series, no reload failures/restarts) but the runbook had no way to catch or bound the same pattern next time — the fleet norm of ≤2 retired objects was known informally, never encoded as a checked threshold.

Update to apply to `rb_metrics_router_canary` (append, do not replace the existing checklist):
- Compare p99 by pod against active and retired generation counts and cleanup-pause durations, per pod.
- Pause additional configuration pushes if retired-generation objects accumulate above 4 per pod, or cleanup pauses exceed 100ms.
- Verify: active-generation consistency, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts.
- Capture generation counts and heap evidence as part of the incident record.
- Responders must not roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered. Rollback remains warranted for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

**How to apply:** Paste the above as additions to `rb_metrics_router_canary`'s existing checklist, keeping its current CPU/memory/queue-depth/route-divergence/dropped-series/restart checks intact. Same "encode the informal fleet norm into a checked threshold" pattern as [[project_canary_safe_staging_doc]]'s ±5%/15-minute pause-trigger formalization. Related unbounded-until-cleanup lineage: [[project_metrics_router_shadow_cache_unbounded_growth]], [[project_metrics_router_matcher_cache_generation_bug]], [[project_metrics_router_matcher_cache_epoch_registry_leak]].

name: project-metrics-router-config-watcher-rename-bug

---

Found 2026-09-18 (observed in staging 2025-07-22 timestamped log): metrics-router's config-watcher subscribes only to `fsnotify.Write` on `routes.yaml`. The deploy pipeline writes a temp file and atomically renames it over `routes.yaml`. This produces a new inode with no `Write` event on the watched path, so the watcher never fires.

**Why:** Staging reproduced this concretely — generation 619 landed on disk via the rename sequence, but the process kept serving stale generation 618 because no `Write` event arrived for the replaced inode. Production is unaffected/unchanged so far (not yet exposed to the same deploy timing, or issue not yet triggered there).

**How to apply:** Fix requires watching `fsnotify.Create`/`Rename` on the parent directory (or re-adding the watch after each event) rather than `Write` on the file path directly, since atomic-rename is the standard safe-config-reload pattern and inode replacement breaks path-based Write-only watches. Related to other [[project_metrics_router_incident_history]] and [[feedback_metrics_router_go_conventions]] items — flag if this needs a canary/rollout plan like other metrics-router fixes.

**Update 2025-07-30:** Revised proposal (git.sphere.internal/infra/metrics-router/pull/1912) keeps the existing `Write` subscription on the routes.yaml inode and adds a 60-second content-hash poll as a fallback to detect atomic replacement — process may keep serving the prior generation for up to that poll interval. New gap found in staging: if the newly detected content fails validation, the branch only emits a debug log with no failed-reload signal (metric/alert), so a bad deploy could silently fail to reload with no operator visibility. Flag this silent-failure gap if/when this PR is reviewed for merge — needs a proper failed-reload signal before shipping.

**Update 2026-09-18:** Requested changes on PR#1912 — poll-based fallback isn't sufficient; asked for real rename/create-aware detection (parent-dir watch or watch re-arm), content-based validation gating publication, a proper failed-reload metric/alert instead of the debug-log-only branch, and a regression test reproducing the original atomic-rename-over-routes.yaml sequence to prove it can't silently serve stale config. Not yet merged.

**Update 2025-08-26:** Owner revised PR#1912 to add directory rename/create handling, pre-publication content validation, and an explicit failed-reload signal — addresses the three prior asks. New stress case surfaces a remaining gap: two atomic replacements 11ms apart cause the first replacement's processing to detach the file watch, so the second replacement is missed until the 60s content-hash poll fires; in that window the process serves the first (now-superseded) generation with no prompt signal that a newer generation was missed on disk. Production unchanged. Still not mergeable as-is — this back-to-back-replacement race needs to be closed before signoff.

**How to apply:** Closed out — no further action needed. On 2024-05-22, reviewed Wes's follow-up revision to the matcher-cache generation fix ([[project_metrics_router_matcher_cache_generation_bug]]) after his earlier raw-pointer reader race attempt was rejected. New version: readers bracket `active.Load()` + `gen.Lookup`/`Match` inside `epochs.Enter()`/`guard.Exit()`; writer swaps `active` and calls `epochs.Retire(old)`, which frees the retired generation only after all reader epochs that started before the swap have drained. Reader-side race looks sound now — no reader can observe a freed generation.

Remaining bug: `BuildGeneration` inserts the candidate into a process-wide `generationRegistry[candidate.ID]` *before* `Validate(candidate)` runs. On validation failure, the code sets `candidate = nil` and returns the error, but never deletes `generationRegistry[candidate.ID]`. Since failed candidates are never published to `active`, they don't affect routing correctness, but every failed reload (e.g. a bad config pushed repeatedly, or a retry loop) leaves a permanent orphaned entry — unbounded registry growth over process lifetime, never garbage collected.

**Why:** Same failure-cleanup-omission pattern as [[project_metrics_router_shadow_cache_unbounded_growth]] (comparator cache never cleared on the failure path) — this is a recurring blind spot in Wes's cache-lifecycle code specifically, not a one-off.

**How to apply:** Fix sent to Wes: either move the `generationRegistry` insert to after `Validate` succeeds, or add `delete(generationRegistry, candidate.ID)` on the validation-failure branch before returning. Flag this pattern (register-before-validate without a failure-path cleanup) if it recurs in future cache/registry PRs from Wes. Wes remains a first-pass reviewer/pairing partner on metrics-router, not its owner ([[project_wes_pairing_metrics_router]]) — do not use this or prior reviews to imply otherwise.

**Update, 2024-05-28 08:36 ET — fix verified and approved:** Wes revised the implementation so candidates are validated before insertion into `generationRegistry`, and every failure path now closes candidate resources explicitly. Published generations still use the epoch guard and retire only after pre-swap reader epochs drain. Evidence: 10,000 repeated invalid reloads with registry size and retained-matcher count flat (6/6, 0/0), and 5M reader-stress iterations with zero post-retirement accesses. User posted a focused approval — reader-lifetime and failed-candidate cleanup fixes accepted, repeated-failure and reader-stress tests kept as required regression tests going forward. Approval explicitly did not extend to ownership: Wes remains first-pass/pairing partner, not metrics-router's owner.

Not yet merged as of 2024-04-25 — check PR status before assuming this landed as specified. Relates to Wes's ongoing metrics-router ramp tracked in [[project_wes_pairing_metrics_router]].

**Update (2024-05-13, post-promotion evidence for release `2024.05.10-rc1`):** fleet-wide production evidence confirms per-generation cache isolation is working as designed — 73 valid config pushes accepted, 2 deliberately stale label-name pushes rejected before activation, and no rejected generation became active anywhere in prod.
